]]><![CDATA[Recent mergers may face investigation following Government error]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/17/recent-mergers-may-face-investigation-following-government-error/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/17/recent-mergers-may-face-investigation-following-government-error/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000Businesses that agreed mergers or takeovers in recent weeks may face investigation by competition regulators as a result of a Government mistake, it has emerged.

Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, Peter Burke, increased the financial values at which mergers must be notified to the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) in July.

However, his department has confirmed that Burke’s order lapsed on September 30th, when it emerged that the Oireachtas had not approved it on time, exposing deals agreed or completed since that date to possible investigation by the commission.

The ministerial order increased the financial threshold at which mergers must be notified to the commission to a combined turnover of €100 million or more, from €60 million.

Competition law obliges the CCPC to investigate deals meeting the threshold to ensure they do not damage competition in their relevant markets, before approving them, often with conditions meant to protect competition.

As the order lapsed on September 30th, the old rules have applied since then.

So mergers or takeovers agreed or completed since then, where the parties’ combined turnover is €60 million or more, and two of those involved have sales of at least €10 million each, may face investigation by the commission.

The CCPC is advising businesses involved in transactions either agreed or completed since September 30th to consider if they meet the old threshold and whether they should notify it of the deal.

The commission pledged not to investigate any parties to deals done in those circumstances for “gun jumping”, that is completing the transactions before getting its approval.

Any mergers completed between July 1st and September 30th were subject to the increased threshold, that is a combined turnover of €100 million or more, and at least €15 million for two of the parties involved.

According to the department, Burke’s order increasing the threshold was laid before the Oireachtas, but did not get the approval of both the Dáil and Seanad within the time set out by the Competition Act, 2002.

“As a result, the order ceased to have effect,” said a spokeswoman, who confirmed that the error emerged following a department review.

The Act requires the CCPC to investigate mergers for their likely impact on competition, but gives the Minster the power to raise the thresholds for such inquiries to keep them in line with inflation and economic circumstances.

Ministerial orders, also dubbed statutory instruments, generally need Oireachtas approval before taking effect.

Burke signed the order on June 10th, branding the move part of his efforts to cut red tape for business.

The Minister said at the time that he increased the financial notification threshold in response to a public consultation that he held earlier this year.

The CCPC favoured an increase as it allowed the regulator to focus resources on deals more likely to have a meaningful impact on competition and consumers.

The last increase was in 2019, before the significant inflation that followed Covid and the war in Ukraine.

The commission has the power to “call in” transactions below the €100 million value where it believes they could affect competition.

The department will work with the CCPC to “progress revised merger notification thresholds at the earliest opportunity in 2027,″ according to its spokeswoman. The law allows only one change each year.

]]>Orla Murray/Coalesce<![CDATA[Withings BodyScan 2 review: Would you spend €500 on keeping tabs on your health? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/10/17/withings-bodyscan-2-review-smart-scale-provides-comprehensive-readings-at-a-hefty-price/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/10/17/withings-bodyscan-2-review-smart-scale-provides-comprehensive-readings-at-a-hefty-price/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000You might have thought that the Withings BodyScan 2 is a simple weighing scale, the type that usually gathers dust in the bathroom because no one really wants – or needs – to weigh themselves on a regular basis.

You would be wrong. This isn’t a scale, it declares. It’s a longevity station. Longevity that will cost you a cool €500.

If you are confused, welcome to the club. I mean, it looks like a scale, albeit a fancy one with a retractable handle that has its own display and a colour screen so you can find out how much of your body it deems is muscle, water and fat, and you can keep track of whatever it is that you feel you need to monitor. But what does that have to with longevity?

A lot, apparently. The BodyScan 2 doesn’t just measure your body composition. It has the equivalent of a six-lead ECG, a blood oxygen sensor, the ability to measure muscle and fat across six zones and monitors the nerves in your feet. There is a lot built into what looks like a fairly standard scales, including metabolic measurements that estimate your basal calorie rate, hypertension notifications and flagging diabetic or heart issues before they become a problem.

It measures vascular age, which looks at the stiffness of your arteries. Not only do they stiffen as you age, but that can also happen as a result of heart disease. The BodyScan 2 measures the speed of the blood pressure wave along the arteries and gives you a score – ideally younger than your heart age, although being in line with your chronological age is considered good.

But I’m getting ahead of myself. The BodyScan 2 has two modes. The first is the daily scan, which is a quick check-in on your weight, body composition and a quick check of your heart and arteries.

The second is the longevity scan, which looks at your metabolic and cardiovascular health. That is scheduled for once a week, although you can take it more regularly if you see the need. That adds the ECG in to the mix, along with nerve response in your feet, and generally takes a little longer on the scale.

You can switch between the two by using the electrodes on the retractable handle as buttons, and all the data is funnelled quickly to the Withings app on your phone for tracking trends etc over wifi.

In measuring body composition, Withings says it is accurate for weight to within 50g and the body fat readings had a 99 per cent correlation to a medical Dexa scan, which is a body composition scan usually used to measure bone density.

Woojer Vest 4 review: This vibrating vest might be the weirdest gadget I’ve ever reviewed

What really made the BodyScan 2 useful for me personally was that it splits your body into six zones – torso, arms, legs and visceral fat – and measures the composition of each. You can see how much muscle and fat is in each area – with the exception of visceral which only measures fat – and see how each has changed over the weeks and months. It avoided labelling me with anything negative (a previous test scale described my body type as “sturdy and obese” and I’ve never recovered from that), instead opting for body profiles that range from “elite” and “powerhouse” to “room to build” and “at risk”. They are colour-coded too, with green, orange and red indicating your rating.

Measuring glucose resilience – a premium feature that comes with a Withings+ subscription – on a scale was a new one for me. The measure reflects how well your body manages your blood sugar, using your visceral fat and nerve response score. The idea is that the Withings system will flag any potential issues before they become a real problem; that is outside the scope of this review, though, as it might take years before it could be tested fully.

All that comes at a stiff price. Withings devices tend to come in at the more premium end of the price scale, and the BodyScan 2 is no exception. But who can put a price on their health? (Withings can, it’s just under €500.)

Good

The BodyScan 2 measures a significant number of data points, from the muscle mass in your legs to your blood oxygen level. Crunch all those numbers into the app and you can get some useful trends and insights that can keep you on the right track to meet your health goals.

It also avoids too many negative labels for body types. “At risk” is the lowest rating for muscle and the highest rating for body fat. Other ratings are “softened” and “robust”, neither of which carry the stigma of the previously mentioned “sturdy and obese” label slapped on my body type by a particularly snarky scale.

Litter Robot 4 review: Fed up with scooping cat litter? Try this

Bad

If you are looking for something simply to measure weight and body composition, this scale is going to be overkill. You can get those measurements from a scale spending less than €50, rather than €500.

Some features are gated behind a subscription, but not any of the essentials.

Everything else

The six-zone measurement also looks at muscle composition, which Withings is pitching not only to those who want to measure their body composition in detail but also for people on GLP-1s to keep an eye on potential muscle loss.

The battery is rechargeable, which means no searching through the junk drawer every few months, and it uses a USB C cable.

Verdict

If you have a need for the extra data and indicators the BodyScan 2 provides, this might be a price you are willing to pay. It might save you money in the long run. But for those who just need the basics, this will be a pricey bathroom addition.

]]><![CDATA[CRH analysts play catch-up as Wall Street braces for rare earnings miss]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/17/crh-analysts-play-catch-up-as-wall-street-braces-for-rare-earnings-miss/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/17/crh-analysts-play-catch-up-as-wall-street-braces-for-rare-earnings-miss/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000The honeymoon is over for CRH chief executive Jim Mintern.

Shares in the building materials and solutions giant jumped more than 40 per cent from the start of his tenure early last year to an all-time high of $131.55 in early January – valuing the business at almost $88 billion (€78 billion).

The rally was fuelled by Mintern’s strategy, unveiled last September, which pledged $40 billion in investment and shareholder returns over five years, alongside annual revenue growth of 7-9 per cent and higher profit margins. Anticipation of the company joining the prestigious S&P 500 index late last year also boosted sentiment, as did a consistent buyer of its shares: CRH itself.

CRH spent $1.2 billion buying back and cancelling its own stock in 2025. It brought the total spent under a repurchase programme that started under Mintern’s predecessor, Albert Manifold, in 2018 to $9.6 billion.

However, the group’s stock has slumped by 40 per cent from those January highs to a low of $78.60 on Wednesday on the New York Stock Exchange, where it moved its main listing two years ago. North America accounted for more than 70 per cent of its earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) last year.

Consensus analysts’ earnings forecasts have trended lower over the course of the year as the Middle East crisis has driven up fuel costs and had a knock-on impact on US house building.

CRH’s energy costs surged more than 17 per cent in the second quarter and were running at an annualised $2.33 billion. The conflict has also sent mortgage rates higher, compounding the affordability problems that were already weighing on US house building.

The average rate on a 15-year fixed-rate mortgage now exceeds 6.7 per cent, up from 5.5 per cent a year ago, according to Freddie Mac, the government-backed mortgage finance company.

With CRH due to unveil its latest quarterly results on October 29th, a number of analysts are beginning to contemplate something rare: an earnings miss from a company with a strong reputation for delivering on its guidance.

Taking a red pen in recent weeks to his forecasts for a host of US construction materials groups, Truist Securities analyst Keith Hughes now sees CRH’s Ebitda coming in at $7.87 billion. While that would mark 2.5 per cent growth on 2025, it would come in below CRH’s own forecast of a figure between $8.1 billion and $8.5 billion.

“The cut at CRH is particularly notable given a long history of hitting numbers, but we now see the possibility of an estimate range reduction,” Hughes warned.

He’s not alone. Shane Carberry of Goodbody, one of the group’s corporate brokers, recently shaved 3 per cent off his Ebitda estimate and now sees it coming in at $7.99 billion. Still, the consensus among analysts, for now, is that CRH will achieve the lower end of its guidance.

Jefferies analysts have said CRH faces “a significant effort” to reach that lower end of its full-year target as cost inflation continues apace. But, for now, they reckon that acquisitions “may bridge the gap”.

Under Manifold, CRH transformed through a series of large acquisitions – and, as importantly, divestments of unwanted assets – from being a business that essentially crushed big rocks into cement, aggregates and asphalt to become a vertically integrated leading infrastructure player in North America.

Mintern has sharpened CRH’s focus even more on what he calls three mega-trends: continuing investment in the transport system, from roads to airports; a need to develop water management; and the re-industrialisation of the US.

AI data centres are among the hottest re-industrialisation plays, with the Trump administration placing them at the heart of America’s industrial revival – betting that they will power the factories of the future and give the US a competitive edge.

Mintern said on a call with analysts in July that CRH was active on 200 data centre projects, with 85 per cent of all current construction in this area within 25 miles of one of the group’s locations.

CRH to buy aggregates operations in Denmark and Finland

The world’s largest five hyperscalers – large-scale cloud computing and technology companies, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle – are expected to spend almost $700 billion this year on US data centres, according to JP Morgan. Construction accounts for about 15 per cent of total development costs.

But while the infrastructure and non-residential construction sectors accounted for more than two-thirds of CRH’s global revenues last year, 32 per cent came from house building, repair and remodelling.

US home completions slumped almost 13 per cent in the first eight months of the year, according to US Census Bureau data. And data for September is due to be reported next Tuesday. With builders grappling with rising interest rates and weak demand, they’re unlikely to provide much relief.

An earnings miss looks more than priced in at CRH, however. The group’s enterprise value – its market capitalisation plus net debt – stands at less than 8.8 times the bottom end of its full-year Ebitda forecast. That leaves the shares trading at a discount of more than 20 per cent to their 10-year median multiple.

Truist’s new price target of $105 for the stock – after cutting its forecasts – points to about 25 per cent upside. The consensus price goal among analysts of $127 suggests more than 50 per cent.

CRH is also poised to tilt further towards infrastructure with the expected completion early next year of its $8.5 billion acquisition of Dallas-based Arcosa – the biggest of more than 1,200 deals in the group’s history.

]]>Eddie Keogh/Imagination<![CDATA[Strike success leaves unions in position of strength and Jack Chambers ‘scrambling’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/10/17/strike-success-leaves-unions-in-position-of-strength-and-jack-chambers-scrambling/https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/10/17/strike-success-leaves-unions-in-position-of-strength-and-jack-chambers-scrambling/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Perhaps nobody in Government had heard the old sales business adage: the first one to name a price always loses.

Now, though, he suggests this week’s industrial unrest might have taken place six years ago, when the public sector pay deal entitled Building Momentum was negotiated, had it not been for the Covid pandemic and the huge uncertainty surrounding almost every aspect of work and the economy at the time.

What made the situation significantly worse over the past year, contributing to the loss of trust for the unions, was the VAT cut to hospitality. This, they felt, was given based on arguments that would not stand up to the scrutiny their own spending proposals are subjected to. Then there was the Government caving to the demands of fuel protesters.

“What you had there,” says one observer on the union side, “was people who went, parked their tractors and trucks and said, ‘right, we have the country by the balls’.”

Another person with a vested interest points to “unelected people suddenly having access to the highest levels of Government and being able to force changes that in some cases had been agreed with elected representatives or people with a respect for democratic structures”.

“Say what you want,” says the first observer, “but unions are regulated, there are rules they have to observe and they do because of the potential consequences.”

Most workers – many in modestly paid jobs and feeling the pinch of rising grocery, fuel and accommodation costs – were more put out by the expiry of the last pay deal in June.

It came at a time when prices were on an upward trajectory but the Government had not indicated when they might get around to ensuring their wages were raised accordingly.

Predictably, there is now something of a blame game as to why talks on a new agreement were delayed beyond the expiry of the last deal in June. What is undisputed is that a couple of exploratory meetings in June went poorly.

By the time Chambers wrote an opinion article in The Irish Times on July 1st, he was suggesting “all issues of importance to both sides can and should be discussed as part of any engagement”. He also warned that “setting preconditions or barriers to engagement does not assist the process of building consensus and agreement”.

The unions indicated early on that they wanted to change what was regarded as the normal running order in previous negotiations and have pay addressed up front.

Fórsa’s Kevin Callinan and John Boyle of the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation have since said they believed pay increases had fallen between 5 and 7 per cent behind inflation over the previous four years. They wanted an agreed plan to close that gap over the lifetime of any new pay deal.

One of those familiar with the process on the Government side suggests the unions wanted a final outcome on the pay issue before anything else could be discussed.

This, they argue, would have left the negotiators on the employer side with no leverage at all as they sought improved productivity through changes to work practice around artificial intelligence (AI), hybrid working or anything else.

There seems to have been surprise among officials that the unions subsequently disengaged, as they viewed it, and proceeded to balloting on industrial action relatively quickly.

The unions express exasperation that Chambers did not intervene directly, pick up the phone or arrange to meet them.

Those with experience of previous pay-agreement negotiations suggest there would traditionally have been more going on by way of back channels.

Callinan’s repeated calls this week for Taoiseach Micheál Martin to get involved are likely rooted in this, it is suggested by veterans of the pre-crash system of engagement during the “social partnership” from 1987 to 2009. Martin, they observe, is the only survivor on the Government side of how that worked and they would like to see his department reassert the control it used to exert over the negotiations.

Martin taking over might not look good for Chambers. However, Callinan made it clear on Friday that the shape of the preliminary talks process was hammed over a call with the Taoiseach.

The unions believe they are in a good position as the process gets under way, given how well Wednesday’s strike went.

Michael Doherty, a professor of law at Maynooth University and a prominent figure in the industrial relations landscape, suggests “the Government may have got a shock by the number of young, enthusiastic people getting a first taste of industrial action on the pickets and anxious to be heard”.

Having energised this young and important constituency, he says the unions need to ensure they do not leave disappointed and disillusioned.

Preventing the second strike should help Chambers and the Government to regain some control over the situation.

To get this far, he has repeatedly said that pay can be talked about at the outset, while the unions have stuck to their position: “Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed.”

Negotiating a deal that is good for the Government will still be a challenge, though.

The unions do not want the sacrifices forced upon them in the wake of that strike 17 years ago to be written out of the equation.

]]>Don Moloney<![CDATA[The Gaeltacht is being destroyed because we won’t build houses]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/17/the-gaeltacht-is-being-destroyed-because-we-wont-build-houses/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/17/the-gaeltacht-is-being-destroyed-because-we-wont-build-houses/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000As winter looms, the evening is so pitch black on Inis Meáin that the few street lights across the sea on Inis Mór make Kilronan look like Manhattan. In the silent night, voices travel, and the low murmur of people chatting leads to the Halla Naomh Eoin, which doubles as the local community centre and the school – the beating heart of the least populated of the Aran Islands.

Inis Meáin hosts one of the country’s few all-Irish boarding schools and it is full of life, always oversubscribed with teenagers enthusiastically embracing island life and its language. Tonight’s meeting is about what will happen in a few years, when these students – both locals and outsiders – become adults, and whether they can settle on the island, rear families, continue to speak Irish and infuse the community with vibrancy.

The impediment on Inis Meáin is housing. Irish-speaking adults who want to live here have few options as prices have gone through the roof for the tiny number of homes that come on the market. Meanwhile, restrictive planning laws mean locals cannot build new homes for their children on their plots.

Ireland’s islands are an essential part of Irishness, an integral part of our heritage and culture and one of the last bastions of Irish as a living, working, breathing, everyday language.

Tonight’s meeting is organised by a group of young Gaeilgeoirí activists called Tinteán (“níl aon tinteán mar do thinteán féin”), whose basic message is that if young Gaeilgeoirí can’t afford to live in the Gaeltacht, it will die very soon. Ironically, we are just a few hundred yards from the cottage where JM Synge spearheaded the Gaelic Revival.

Without people, there is no revival.

According to the latest census, the country’s island population has fallen below 3,000 for the first time. To put this into context, in 1841 there were 48,000 people living on the islands off the western seaboard. Today the average age on the islands is 59 - in contrast to the rest of the country, where it is 43 – and more than one in five of the islands’ population are aged 65 years and older.

The crucial age group between 20 and 35 accounts for just 7.9 per cent of the islands’ population, as opposed to 25 per cent for the State as a whole.

Meanwhile, just 5 per cent of the islands’ population is under four years old, compared with an average of 8 per cent nationally.

These population dynamics mean only one thing: catastrophic decline and, along with a disappearing population, a disappearing language and culture. What would Synge think?

It is essential that the population decline is reversed. At a time when the Irish language has rarely been more popular, when thousands of people are learning and in some cases relearning it, the Gaeltacht itself is being destroyed by the refusal to do the very thing that generations of people from the west of Ireland did all over the world: build houses. Young families make communities, and if they have no places to live then the community dies or becomes more like a museum – visited by curious onlookers during the holiday season, but for all intents and purposes, dead.

One of the main issues is that homes have become trophy assets. When a house here comes up for sale, it is marketed online to everyone from London to New York to Mount Merrion. There is a burgeoning national and international market for property in the west of Ireland, and this process elbows out the local people, pushing prices way out of reach for the average islander.

In addition, the tourist market, so long the source of summer income, has changed dramatically.

Airbnb and Booking.com have made it so attractive for property owners to rent out their places short term that these potential homes are taken off the rental market for young Gaeilgeoirí who can’t afford to compete in trophy auctions. In many cases they are being given the option to rent until the summer comes, and then weekly rents skyrocket for the tourist season and the families must find somewhere else to live until September. They are in effect school-year residents, and that oddly nomadic existence rarely encourages people to put down roots.

Naturally, as more and more rural hotels have been turned over to refugees, tourist bed capacity falls, putting more pressure on the existing housing stock.

Life on Inis Meáin: ‘Some people will say there’s nothing here, but in fact there is everything here’

Another issue is vacancy – and ultimately dereliction, because an uninhabited house doesn’t stand a chance against Atlantic storms for long. For example, according to the local community office, on Inis Meáin there are 149 houses, of which 65 are uninhabited. Nearly half of all the homes on an island with a housing crisis stand empty.

So what can be done?

We know that people respond to incentives, positive and negative. With respect to building houses in the Gaeltacht to enable Gaeilgeoir families to live here, the key is to create the incentives to make the local housing market work. Considering the fact that there are vacant houses on the island, what might make the owners put them on the market?

At the moment, capital gains must be paid if you sell a vacant property. This is an obvious impediment to selling. Why go through the hassle of selling, particularly an old family house split between a few children, if the government gets 31 per cent of the profit? What about specifically cancelling capital gains on the islands in order to lubricate supply? Make it easy to sell. Such a move would change the conversation about selling.

A buyer’s tax break, specifically for Gaeilgeoirí, like the Temple Bar tax breaks for residents in the 1990s, would bias buying to Irish speakers.

On the planning side, what about setting a quantity of homes to be built by locals every year, based on demand and family structure, allowing the residents to solve their own problems? This would give local people the ability to build on their own island, for their own community.

‘It’s just like a match made in heaven’: Family of seven who moved to Inis Meáin urge others to follow

Even if these initiatives were embraced, there is still the issue of the cost of island life – which is far in excess of anything on the mainland. Those of us who don’t live on small islands don’t realise that the sea is a big cost driver. Think about getting material to the island, renting the truck to bring the materials to the harbour on the mainland, renting the boat to bring the stuff across, finding the workers to do the job, putting them up while they are working, and so on. All these things cost money, yet the income of Ireland’s islanders is far below the national average.

What about making island life tax-free for Gaeilgeorí, treating the people the way we treat US multinational capital? When we cut corporation tax, activity responded. The same would apply with income tax, excise duty and VAT on islands.

If we are talking about the Gaeltacht and the language, what about making living on the island tax free for Gaeilgeori? The sums of money would be tiny for a country with an annual budget of €147 billion. We are talking about only a few thousand people initially. The cost is minuscule and the prize, the preservation of a way of life and a language that has been spoken continuously in this part of the country for more than 2,500 years, is enormous.

This morning I asked a local about the weather and he responded, “Tá sé leathghlas ceart go leor,” or, “It’s a bit half grey all right.” (Down here glas isn’t green, it’s grey.) The half grey refers to the sea, the sky and heavy clouds, and the colour of the rocks, the limestone and the horizon where the sea and the clouds meet in a misty angry grey haze. This linguistic richness comes from hundreds of generations inscribing their language with colour, significance and their own meaning.

Imagine losing this for the sake of a few pennies.

Other valuation metrics tell a similar story. Apple trades on 36 times estimated earnings, well above its five-year average of 27.

Apple is pricey not only relative to its own history but to all but one of its magnificent seven peers (Tesla, of course). For historical reasons, 65 ended up as the widely accepted retirement age, but for a large part of human history, there was no such thing as formal retirement. People simply worked until they became incapable of doing so.

We have Bismarck to thank for introducing the concept of a modern state pension in the 19th century, with the retirement age set at 70 – at a time when few enough people lived to see that age. It was also 70 when the Old Age Pensions Act came into force in Ireland in 1908.

The qualifying age was subsequently adjusted downwards to where we are today, although a report produced in May of this year for the Financial Planning Standards Board suggests that while it’s nominally 65, many Irish people now expect to work until the age of 70 to maintain their standard of living.

Almost 80 per cent of those surveyed also felt financially unprepared for retirement, with a critical knowledge gap between what they were putting into their pension fund and how much income they thought that fund would provide when the time came.

Money, or having enough of it, pretty much tops the lists of concerns voiced by those facing retirement. This is closely followed by anxiety about filling the time previously taken up by work.

“Money is terribly important and, in an ideal world, you would start thinking about it long before you retire, maybe seven to 10 years before the planned date, because the sanest and most tax-effective way to save for retirement is by contributing to a pension scheme,” says Paul Kenny, a veteran of the pensions industry and Ireland’s first pensions ombudsman, who now leads courses for the Retirement Planning Council designed to get people retirement fit.

“Things happen that can radically change when people retire, such as illness, redundancy or an accident,” Kenny says. “Then there are those who put things on the long finger and suddenly they’re facing retirement with no financial plan.

“But all is not lost. Last-minute additional voluntary contributions (AVCs) are an option. How much you can put in is limited by your income in the final year and how much you can claim against tax, but they’re worth considering,” Kenny says.

AVCs are supplementary payments into your pension fund. If you’re in your late fifties, you can get tax relief on as much as 35 per cent of your salary if you put it into your pension fund. Above 60, that percentage jumps to 40 per cent.

So if you have just turned 60 and are earning €90,000, with normal pension contributions of 6 per cent, or €5,400, you can put up to a further €30,600 into your pension, assuming you have it. For many, it is a way of beefing up retirement income in a tax-efficient manner if they come into a windfall, such as an inheritance.

“When you’re looking at your overall money picture, an awful lot also depends on what kind of pension scheme you’re in because, in some cases, if you’re already getting the maximum from a scheme, AVCs are not going to do you any good. So, you need to know what you’re in and the benefits,” Kenny says.

“Annuities and approved retirement funds (ARFs) may also come up when discussing retirement financial planning,” Kenny adds. Both are products related to after-retirement income, not saving for retirement.

“An annuity, which will guarantee a payment for your lifetime, will be bought from an insurance company with the money in your pension fund and will very much tie you to what are currently low interest rates. Annuities are based on life expectancy and bond yields, and if interest rates are low, bond yields are low, so you’re locking yourself into a low interest rate for life.

“With ARFs, rather than lock your money into an annuity at a point in time, it remains invested after your retirement, with the retiree drawing down a certain portion of the fund each year.

“It’s crucial how you invest the money because that’s what will determine the capacity to draw down over the rest of your life. So, it’s really important to get good advice.

“ARFs are generally run by insurance companies, and they’re investing in massive numbers of different assets all over the world, something you could never do on your own, and this spreads the risk. They pay you the monies you are drawing down and take care of things like PAYE. An ARF gives you flexibility; if you really need money, you can make a drawdown and pay the necessary tax.”

Kenny says that the one thing to watch with ARF investments is the charges.

“If you’re being offered ‘hello money’ in the form of a bonus allocation, be careful. There’s only one person paying for that. So, the message is to go for the lowest charges. Anything over 1 per cent should be viewed with suspicion.”

Assuming the money side of things is under control, the next burning question for many prospective retirees is what to do with their time.

The psychosocial infrastructure is the term used to describe what a community, such as a workplace, provides to the individual. For better or for worse, this means having colleagues, work to do, and company events to attend. Losing this infrastructure can be a difficult adjustment, especially for those who have been defined by their job (often those in senior positions and the professions) or in whose life work was the dominant feature.

Kenny suggests reframing “all the time I have on my hands” to see it as a bonus, not a negative. “You’re getting back 50+ hours a week and why would you sit there and twiddle your thumbs when there is so much you could do?” he says.

“First of all, some people still want to work, so explore the options. Can you continue to work with reduced hours or part-time at your existing company with less pressure?

“Often people don’t want to keep doing what they’ve done for years, but that shouldn’t be a deterrent to doing something else. It’s really a question of looking for what’s available. If someone is prepared to work voluntarily rather than needing paid employment, then that opens another avenue.

“Sharing your talents, life and work skills with others can be invaluable and it feels good to give back. There are many charitable organisations which would bite your hand off if you had the skills to revamp an outdated system or update a website, for example.”

Retirees often get asked to join a board and, for many, it’s a good way of staying in touch. However, Kenny raises a warning flag. “Check the number of subcommittees because what looks like a once-a-month commitment can suddenly become twice a week,” he says.

Kenny adds age-appropriate exercise into the retiree timetable and also something to keep the brain agile. Both learning a new language and taking up a musical instrument for the first time are seen as particularly good ways to challenge the grey matter.

“The education and training boards offer a huge variety of hobby and other courses, with many of them heavily subsidised and run during the day. Then there are the more formal courses at Third Level for those who want to go the academic route,” Kenny says.

“Then come the hobbies which split into things you do alone and things you do with other people. I know of a gentleman who retired at 76 having known nothing but farming all his life. His son convinced him to go on a retirement planning course, and since then he has taken up horticulture, baking bread, general cookery, hill walking, yoga and line dancing.

“The wonderful thing about any of these activities is that they bring you into contact with new people who have no idea about who you are based on what you used to do,” Kenny adds. “In a sense, you get your personal identity back, and maybe that’s still a 25-year-old trying to break loose.”

]]>Halfpoint<![CDATA[House prices: Who is getting it right, the CSO, MyHome or Daft?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/16/the-cso-myhome-or-daft-whos-right-on-house-prices/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/16/the-cso-myhome-or-daft-whos-right-on-house-prices/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000In the lead-up to the property crash of 2008 there was – let’s just say – unease about the number of estate agencies publishing what you might call self-interested house-price surveys.

Critics said their reports, and some of the commentary that went with them, were deliberately amplifying positive trends to encourage transactions.

When things began to sour, the “endless growth” narrative around Irish property gave way to the soft-landing narrative: “Okay, things have got a little frothy, there will be a modest correction, but the market is still structurally sound.”

When that thesis collapsed, and Ireland suffered the biggest peak-to-trough property crash of any country, property-price surveys (industry ones) were blamed for exacerbating the problem.

The task of producing an accurate data series on property price trends was given to the Central Statistics Office (CSO). In 2011 the agency began producing the Residential Property Price Index (RPPI), which remains the State’s official indicator of price trends.

A decade and a half later the industry barometers have crept back into the mix, led by the State’s two main property portals: MyHome and Daft. (MyHome is owned by The Irish Times Group).

While both companies’ quarterly reports are viewed as highly credible, they contain structural biases. Foremost, they base their quarterly surveys on asking prices rather than sold prices. In a sellers’ market, where buyers can get into bidding wars, these metrics can underestimate prices. The reverse is true when the market turns.

“From 2024 through to the spring of this year, transaction prices rose faster than list prices, and buyers typically paid well over the list price,” author of the Daft report Ronan Lyons said in the company’s latest survey.

Irish house prices are simply too high, and potential buyers have hit a price ceiling

“That has now reversed. Nationally, list prices are rising over two percentage points faster than transaction prices, the widest gap since 2023,” he said.

While Daft commands a larger market share of listings nationally, Daft and MyHome are said to be neck and neck (in terms of the listings market) in Dublin and Leinster, with most listings on both portals coming from estate agents.

Are we turning a corner on housing?

There are also quarterly surveys from Sherry Fitzgerald, Douglas Newman Good (DNG) and the Real Estate Alliance (REA), which use different methodologies.

At the moment they all tell the same story: house prices are still rising but at a slower pace than before because of a combination of affordability pressures linked to higher inflation, higher borrowing costs, enhanced supply and the uncertain economic outlook.

Further interest rate hikes and no resolution to the Iran crisis are likely to accelerate this trend.

Daft’s snapshot of the market in the third quarter put headline annualised inflation (for asking prices) at 3 per cent, half the level that it was a year ago. In Dublin the rate of price growth was estimated at 2.7 per cent.

MyHome’s equivalent report, published on Tuesday this week, put asking price inflation at 3.9 per cent and at 2.1 per cent in Dublin.

The CSO’s official numbers, also published on Tuesday, put inflation (for prices paid) at 5.1 per cent in August and at 3.9 per cent in Dublin.

The CSO’s numbers are based on stamp duty data from Revenue and reflect transactions that took place at least two months ago, so there’s a lag. Because they are based on asking prices, the MyHome and Daft reports provide more of an instant snapshot of which way the market is turning.

The CSO estimates the average price paid for a property nationally in the 12 months to August was €442,512, while in Dublin it was €598,677.

For MyHome, the average price nationally was €461,084 and €585,132 in Dublin. For Daft, the figures were €445,000 and €635,000.

The CSO and MyHome use median (middle value) prices in their reports instead of average prices.

With any property price survey, there is a need to distinguish between quality-adjusted price changes [those controlled for location, property type, new versus old homes, etc] and pure price inflation.

The CSO breaks its figures down by Eircode, which reveals significant price disparities not just between Dublin and the rest of the State but also within the capital itself.

Take, for example, the difference between Dublin 6, which covers Ranelagh and Rathgar, where the average price paid for properties last year was just shy of €1 million (€995,709), making it the most expensive Eircode in the State, and Dublin 10, which includes Ballyfermot and Cherry Orchard, where the average price was €333,391.

Irish house price inflation slows as affordability constraints bite

According to MyHome, house prices in Tuam in Galway have risen by 10.2 per cent in 2026 while prices in Kilkee in Clare have slumped by almost 13 per cent.

So while the CSO, MyHome and Daft capture the general direction of travel, they can differ significantly because of the disparity between asking prices and actual sale prices.

Put another way, MyHome and Daft measure what sellers want; the CSO measures what buyers actually pay.

What’s the point of Ifac?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/what-is-the-point-of-ifac-if-the-coalition-just-ignores-its-warnings/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/what-is-the-point-of-ifac-if-the-coalition-just-ignores-its-warnings/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 04:15:00 +0000All bark and no bite. If you wanted to be cruel about Ireland’s so-called fiscal watchdog – that would be the obvious cliche to throw its way.

For years, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (Ifac) has advised successive ministers for finance to go easy on the spending increases and tax cuts, put away more money and account properly for the possibility of overruns.

Yet, time and again on budget day, much of the advice appears to be quietly ignored.

Take Budget 2027, for example.

The budgetary process now begins several months before the big day itself – with the Stability Programme Update in April, followed by the Summer Economic Statement (SES) in July. Between them, the two documents provide a good sense of what will be at the Government’s disposal later in the year.

In August, after having a good look at the SES, which outlined the broad parameters for the budget, Ifac said the economy did not need any budgetary support.

It said the economy continued to grow at a “remarkable pace” even when the distorting impact of the multinationals was stripped out of the official figures.

Casting his eye across the SES’s implied net spending growth, its chairman Seamus Coffey said the plans were “not appropriate” for an economy in such a strong position.

Ifac’s position was that if the Government continued down this road, then its policies would only add to an already worrying inflation outlook.

And what did the Government do?

Within hours of the budget’s publication, Ifac said it had put “the public finances on a worse trajectory by repeatedly breaking established spending limits and increasingly relying on high-risk corporation tax”.

Budget puts public finances on worse trajectory, watchdog warns

Coffey noted that, rather than heed the warnings, the Government was planning on spending €6 out of every €7 in corporation tax it collected.

The Government, as would be expected, defended the €8.7 billion in new measures. Minister for Finance Simon Harris had already defined the respective roles as he saw it.

“We don’t ignore their advice, but they’re not the Government,” he said.

So what is the continued point of having an institution set up in the wake of the 2008 crash to prevent a re-run of that calamity if modern-day governments choose not to take its advice?

Michael McMahon, a professor of macroeconomics, sat on the council for nearly seven years before serving as interim chairman between 2023 and 2024.

“When I joined, I thought we’d actually be advising the Government,” he says.

“That we’d go and meet the ministers involved and say, ‘This is a nonsensical policy; we think this would be better’. I thought it would be technocratic, geeky advice on the highest levels.”

Instead, McMahon quickly realised it was Ifac’s role to assess what was being proposed. “You could replace the word ‘advisory’ in Ifac’s name with ‘assessment’,” he says.

While chairman in 2023, McMahon added his voice to those of his predecessors, warning that the government risked “repeating Ireland’s past mistakes” with its upcoming budget. In particular, the tendency to breach its own spending rule had bothered the council members.

At the time, he said the State was over-reliant on windfall corporation tax revenues in the same way pre-crash governments had relied on property-related taxes.

How Budget 2027 will impact families: From renters to stay-at-home parents

McMahon also entertained the idea that, at some point in the future, Ifac could hit the “big red button” available to it and refuse to endorse budgetary forecasts. He said the council would be more likely to “wield big sticks” if the spending breaches were going to be repeated year after year.

Looking back, did his words and those of the other Ifac members have any impact?

“The question is not whether the government has always exactly complied with the letter of the recommendations,” he says.

“But rather, what would have happened with spending and tax decisions if an institution like the fiscal council was not endorsing the macro forecasts and criticising the decisions being made?”

McMahon says it is likely, in his view, that government spending would have been higher- and potentially riskier – had it not been for the role played by Ifac over a number of years.

During his time on the council, the government consistently ignored its own spending growth cap of 5 per cent annually, exceeding it each time.

However, the economist claims the cap may not have been introduced at all or, if it had, it would have been exceeded by an even greater margin had there been no independent oversight.

McMahon also says it is his belief that the Future Ireland Fund (FIF) – the sovereign wealth fund into which the Government is investing 0.8 per cent of GDP annually – may not have come about had it not been for persistent calls for such a plan from Ifac.

“I think Ifac is useful; it has shifted the debate in Ireland. I don’t think we would have the FIF without it,” he says.

Ifac was established during the bailout years, when the country was picking up the pieces from an economic crash that pushed us into a three-year IMF-EU bailout.

Cut costs and abolish Ifac

Ireland had narrowed its tax base during the Celtic Tiger era and was badly caught out when the international banking crisis coincided with a collapse in house prices. An over-dependence on elements like stamp duty left public finances cruelly exposed.

Ifac, it appeared, was designed to remind policymakers that the same mistakes could not be repeated. Promoting fiscal responsibility seemed to be its overarching mission.

John Moran was secretary general at the Department of Finance between 2012 and 2014 when Ifac first got up and running. The terms of the bailout hung over the government, and the council was, at times, insistent on difficult medicine.

“We were in a tough position of trying to bring the budget back into order,” he says.

“There would have been moments of disagreement [with Ifac], where perhaps the political judgment of the government at the time was that they needed to do things that were seen as more politically palatable to keep the coalition together and keep the public onside.”

Moran says the economic landscape nowadays, in some ways, is comparable to the pre-crisis years.

“Today’s world is in a different position,” he says. “There are questions about how much extra spending you can do; that’s where the contrast lies [with the bailout years].

“We have some parallels between now and the situation before when we got into financial difficulties, with very concentrated tax sources.”

Budget 2027: Big business pays the bills as Coalition rolls the dice

The first chairman of Ifac was Prof John McHale.

He believes its importance lies in being able to publicise a counterpoint to government policy. Much of the time, he says, what Ifac is stating is not entirely different from what senior civil servants are telling ministers behind the scenes.

“It is different from [saying] it in public. In a way it helps the government – it helps balance the debate,” McHale says.

“You would never expect the government would take on what we would advise wholesale – it’s under huge political pressure. The council’s role was to take on a longer-term view. We were pulling in very different directions.”

So what was the relationship like between the government and Ifac?

“On the whole, it was good. Sometimes they were a little less forthcoming with information than the council would have liked, and it made our job harder,” he says.

That inability to always get the information it wants from civil servants could be solved, says McHale, by granting Ifac a statutory right. He points out that the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has again recently called for this.

That report also highlighted the relative lack of resources available to the council.

Applauding its ability to shape the media narrative here, the OECD said the body “punches above its weight”. It said Ifac ranked highly among similar bodies in other countries and had an ability to “generate influence despite limited resources”.

While winning plaudits from external reviewers, some politicians have eyed Ifac with a little suspicion over the years.

At a time when Ireland was crying out for public investment, particularly in housing, it has been accused of sometimes offering a narrow and needlessly cautious prescription. Yes, the argument went, the economy is doing well, but there are huge gaps where more money should also be spent.

How can runaway spending in the health service be reined in?

Sinn Féin’s spokesman on finance, Pearse Doherty, says there could be “question marks” over some of Ifac’s warnings down through the years, which were perhaps “too conservative”.

“If we look back at Ifac’s recommendations – and they have gone unheeded by the government in the past – the economy has still continued to grow and continued to have surpluses,” he says.

However, he says the council has played an important role over recent budgets in highlighting consistent spending overruns.

“Ifac have focused – and I think they have been misrepresented in my own view – on the government’s unplanned spending,” he says.

“It undermines the budget day process. You have a situation where the government announces X amount of spending on budget day, but by the end of the year, that has gone up due to unplanned measures.”

Doherty says he doesn’t know what Ifac would have to say about his party’s budget plans. But he believes it would be in line with Ifac’s current thinking on how the funding of extra spending should be done through the raising of additional tax revenues.

“The big difference between us and the Government is that we would increase capital expenditure,” he says. “I’m not sure what view they (Ifac) would take in relation to that.”

The other question that gets thrown at the “watchdog” is whether it is still needed, given that bodies such as the Central Bank of Ireland and the ESRI frequently offer similar criticisms of budgetary policy. The groupthink that prevailed in the pre-crisis period, so the argument goes, is no longer a problem.

With so much cash sloshing around, why is there a housing crisis?

“It is certainly true that there is a lot of common ground between the ESRI, the council and the Central Bank,” says McHale.

“It makes a difference when you have a body that has a statutory role in assessing these things. The Government has to respond to the council’s report; that is what really makes it stand out.”

McHale, though no longer part of Ifac, believes that budgetary policy is in a “reasonable place”. Despite criticisms around the nature of windfall taxes, he says it remains important that the Government is still running surpluses, though he’d like these to be higher.

This would be wise, he says, “given the underlying risks we face”.

McMahon says Ifac is more about “shaping thinking than shaping policies” and it fits the role of a “town crier”.

“We would all love 10 per cent growth a year, and everyone get free cookies,” he says.

“But we all know the pain that comes from reckless fiscal policy, and there is generally more pain than there is fun on the upside.”

]]>Provision<![CDATA[The rich are getting richer, so why no wealth tax?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/15/the-rich-are-getting-richer-so-why-no-wealth-tax/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/15/the-rich-are-getting-richer-so-why-no-wealth-tax/Thu, 15 Oct 2026 12:03:13 +0000Around the world, the rich are getting richer, with soaring stock markets and other asset values lining their pockets. So why – in most countries – is there no wealth tax?

True, most tax systems do tax wealth in specific ways, such as charges on property or capital gains. But straight-up wealth taxes – an annual charge on the value of the assets held – are rare.

But with exchequers worldwide searching for cash, taxing wealth is coming back on to the agenda. A new report from the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) crunches the numbers and outlines the key choices facing Irish policymakers.

It shows there is a lot of wealth in Ireland that could be taxed, but raising a significant amount of money requires big political decisions.

For Ireland, as for other countries, the choice is whether a wealth tax would be for show – a political signal that the wealthiest should pay a bit more – or for dough, in other words to raise a significant amount of money for the exchequer.

Higher wealth – fewer wealth taxes

One of the peculiarities of recent years is that although the wealth of the billionaire class has risen worldwide, the number of countries with wealth taxes has shrunk.

The ESRI report points out that 12 European countries levied an annual tax on net wealth in 1990 compared with only Norway, Spain and Switzerland last year.

Low revenue yields, administrative challenges and concerns that capital would move to other countries are among the reasons cited for countries abandoning the taxes.

France abolished its wealth tax in 2018, citing fears of wealth moving out of the country, and replaced it with a tax on real estate worldwide assets valued at more than €1.3 million. Despite rising wealth, the key message is that full-scale wealth taxes are not easy to design and implement.

Wealth in Ireland

Household wealth in Ireland, as measured by the Central Statistics Office household finance and consumption survey in 2023, was €927 billion, about two-and-a-half-times higher than a decade earlier.

That is an average (median) net wealth of just under €256,000 per household, with the family home the main asset for the vast majority. Where a mortgage is still outstanding, this is subtracted from the net wealth figures.

The story of Irish assets over the past decade can be told in a few headlines – rising house prices are the key factor, followed by lower household debt as the Celtic Tiger loans are paid down and a rise in business assets among the better off.

The top 10 per cent still controls close to 50 per cent of wealth. It is worth noting, also, that separate Central Bank of Ireland data, which showed wealth at just over €1 billion early 2023 – a bit higher than the CSO – estimated it at being more than €1.42 billion in the first quarter of this year.

Taxing questions

Assets are taxed in Ireland via a few routes, notably capital gains tax and capital acquisitions tax on inheritance and gifts.

However, even if you add the amounts collected via these taxes to stamp duty and local property tax – which operates more like a charge – the total revenue comes to less than €6 billion in 2025 out of total tax revenue of more than €105 billion. Could a wealth tax increase the revenue significantly?

Well, it depends. The key insight from the ESRI paper was that if an Irish wealth tax was going to raise significant money, then it would have to have a wide base – in other words most assets would have to be included. If this happened, then even if the tax kicked in at relatively high wealth levels, significant sums could be raised.

The political problem is that a broad base takes in areas such as businesses, farms and the family home. If all wealth in the State were taxed at 1 per cent, the yield would be €9.3 billion based on the 2023 figures and probably more than €10 billion now. This is not a realistic scenario, but it provides a kind of benchmark.

The researchers go through a range of scenarios, with the widest possible tax base, one excluding the family home and a narrow definition including mainly financial assets and investment property. Cut-off points above which wealth would be taxed range from €250,000 to €2 million, with these figures doubled for a married couple. In all cases the tax rate is 1 per cent and pensions are excluded.

Three lessons

The first – and most striking – lesson is the importance of the range of assets covered. Exempting the family home, businesses and farms cuts the pot significantly.

At a threshold of €500,000 for example – which would be €1 million for a married couple – a narrow base just including financial assets and other investments would raise less than €450 million annually, while one including all assets would raise close to €3 billion.

The second lesson is not surprising: it is that as the threshold lowers for the wealth level where the tax kicks in, the numbers rise sharply.

At the €500,000 threshold, 4.5 per cent of households have to pay. At the lowest one, €250,000, it rises to more than a third. But the share of total national wealth rises less sharply – from 19 per cent to 32 per cent – as the amount of assets held per household falls sharply at lower levels.

The third lesson reflects the importance of the family home as the source of wealth for middle and higher earners. The main residence is only a small portion of wealth at the very highest level – where households typically own businesses or have significant financial asset. For middle Ireland, the family home is the key asset.

For a wealth tax covering everyone with assets over €250,000, exempting the family home would cut the annual tax take from €4.5 billion to €2.6 billion.

Who pays?

The profile of those who pay depends crucially on the rules set. The wealthiest top 10 per cent will always be hit hardest, but a key political decision would be where to draw the line. Too high and you limit the revenue raised. Too low and it ends up as a family home tax on middle earners.

The fact that there are wealthy people with relatively low incomes is another complication.

Overall, an Irish wealth tax would mainly hit middle-aged and older property owners – those aged 55 years of age plus would pay about two-thirds of the tax under most scenarios. If the base of the tax is narrow – excluding the family home – then those aged 65 or more would be in the firing line as those hold higher investments in savings and other financial assets.

They would typically paying close to half or more of the total tax, depending on the rules. On the flip side, younger renters hold hardly any wealth, so would pay little tax.

The bottom line

The report underlines that a wealth tax could raise a significant sum in revenue, but only if it covered a broad base of wealth.

This brings politically sensitive areas of business and farm wealth and the family home into the picture – all advantaged by the Irish tax system at present. An alternative, as recommended by the Commission on Tax and Welfare in 2023, is to increase existing taxes on wealth rather that introducing a separate new wealth tax.

But there is no easy decisions either here for Irish politicians – do they, for example, end the favourable inheritance rules for businesses and farms? Or hike local property tax?

None of these things will happen for as long as there is a budget surplus. But with the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council warning that more revenue will be needed in the years ahead to meet the costs of an ageing population and climate change, sooner or later Irish policymakers will have to consider where it comes from.

Sinn Féin has called for a study on a wealth tax and recommended hikes on capital taxes and pensions. Labour’s alternative budget also calls for a hike in a range of capital taxes, including capital gains tax and the capital acquisitions tax.

The Social Democrats want to tax the “super-wealthy”, likely only to work as part of an international drive in this area, while People Before Profit also want to “tax the multi-millionaires.”

But more taxes on wealth are now creeping on to the Irish political agenda. The comfortable classes are in the firing line – even if they don’t realise it yet.

The ECB has already pushed through two quarter-of-a-percentage-point rate increases since the middle of June.

NTMA sells €1.25bn of bonds amid market turmoil

Other dynamics have also been at play in the European debt markets in recent times. Investors have been increasingly demanding higher rates for French and Italian debt, relative to Germany, the main euro-zone benchmark, amid concerns about their high, and rising, debt levels.

The yield on 10-year French bonds reached 4.9 per cent earlier this week, amid market concerns about political instability hampering efforts to bring the country’s budget deficit under control. France is heading into a presidential election next spring.

The difference – or spread – between the yields on 10-year French and German bonds high 1.59 percentage points earlier this month, the widest since November 2011, at the height of the euro-zone sovereign-debt crisis.

Italy’s €3-trillion government bond market, one of the world’s biggest, has ​come under renewed scrutiny amid contagion from a sharp sell-off in French debt. Bond yields move inversely to bond prices.

Italian 10-year bond rates hit 4.7 per cent this month and the yield gap with safe-haven German bunds reached its widest in almost 18 months.

Italy’s national election next year throws doubt on Rome’s plans to reverse the rise in ‌its huge public debt, according to analysts. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg

]]>Imen Ben Youssef<![CDATA[The global economy and the art of living dangerously]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/15/the-global-economy-and-the-art-of-living-dangerously/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/15/the-global-economy-and-the-art-of-living-dangerously/Thu, 15 Oct 2026 13:30:00 +0000The past few days have reminded us of one of the two chief contemporary economic realities: the president of the US is a wrecker.

Yet this is consistent with the other reality, which is that despite the disruptions and shocks of our era, the world economy remains a powerful growth machine, driven by remarkable innovations, risk-taking finance and large accumulations of debt. Can this last?

The reason for believing it will is that growth has been the dominant feature of the global economy since the middle of the last century. Yet we must always remember that growth is one thing, but stable growth quite another.

What, then, is the latest US president Donald Trump outrage? First, he started a war on Iran, without a plan, which has raised diesel prices in the US and worldwide. Then, a few days ago, he made a deal with Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel on global markets, in violation of sanctions imposed after Putin’s illegal invasion of Ukraine.

Trump also told Kyiv to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and threatened to cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine and access to US-made weapons.

This “deal” is both foolish and wicked: foolish, because it is too small to lower diesel prices significantly, and wicked, because it is prepared to sacrifice a country that is struggling heroically to be free from tyranny.

Current US policymaking is not just reckless and immoral. It is also one of the causes of the world’s unpredictability.

Thus, the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) latest World Economic Outlook (WEO) starts with the following comment from Silvana Tenreyro, the new economic counsellor: “In less than seven years, the global economy has been subjected to an exceptional sequence of events.”

Current US policymaking is not just reckless and immoral. It is also one of the causes of the world’s unpredictability.

Yet all but one of these shocks, the exception being the pandemic, are man-made, or perhaps “strongman-made”. The others are the war in Ukraine, the tariff war and the war in the Middle East. Putin launched the first of these in 2022. Trump, of course, began the other two.

These shocks have, as Tenreyro says, “tested the resilience of households, firms, financial markets and governments. Individually, each of these big developments would have been considered unlikely. Their confluence over such a short period of time is even more extraordinary.”

Yet, remarkably, the WEO’s forecasts for growth this year and next, at 3.1 and 3.4 per cent respectively, are “broadly unchanged from April”, despite more persistent energy disruption than was then expected.

Global inflation is, however, expected to hit 4.7 per cent this year, as a result of higher commodity prices, and 4.1 per cent in 2027. But, happily, “the pass-through to core inflation is expected to be limited”.

The explanations for this resilience are familiar. They include adjustment of exports and imports away from direct trade between the US and China. More recently, however, the dominant factors have been the flexibility of the global energy economy, discussed here last week, and the investment boom triggered by artificial intelligence (AI).

Yet neither is guaranteed to last. As Nick Butler points out, stocks of crude and products are low after six months of drawdowns. Moreover, “product exports of diesel and jet fuel [from the Gulf] remain minimal”. Also at risk are supplies of naphtha, urea and liquefied natural gas (the latter of special importance to Europe).

The AI investment boom also concentrates risk. Even if AI itself works out, the level of investment is likely to stop growing, if not decline, at some point. Moreover, AI might not work out financially on the hoped-for scale at all.

Other fragilities are evident, notably the fiscal positions. Despite the big post-pandemic rise in real and nominal interest rates, most large economies continue to run significant primary fiscal deficits (before interest payments).

It would help if the shocks stopped, too. Alas, given our leaders, I would not bet on that.

The US position stands out, with a forecast primary fiscal deficit of 4.8 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, a share of T-bill issuance in gross borrowing at 58 per cent and an average maturity of a mere 5.9 years.

The WEO rightly emphasises the importance of rebuilding fiscal space. The good news is that, in today’s circumstances, the negative impact of structural fiscal tightening is likely to be offset by lower real and nominal interest rates. But redressing global current accounts imbalances will also be essential. That must, at last, involve China.

Ireland is richer and spending more than 30 years ago but is it making us happy?

The WEO emphasises other downside risks, including a worsening of the ongoing wars, (probably AI-enhanced) cyber threats and climate catastrophes.

Neither a stock market crash nor a collapse in AI-related investment can be ruled out, should returns on AI disappoint. Upside economic risks include still faster progress with AI technology, though that could also inflict devastating social consequences.

Another plausible upside is an accelerated energy transition, as recent events underline the unreliability of fossil fuels. Given their physical location, these are bound to remain so for many countries.

John FitzGerald: Budget reversal of policy on tackling climate change was a mistake

The WEO notes that the ability to exploit AI and meet energy needs reliably will be crucial for growth prospects. Sadly, the world’s poorest countries are particularly vulnerable in both respects. Thus, the WEO rightly fears that their living standards are likely to fall still farther behind those in richer countries.

It would be good to believe the world will become less prone to shocks. But it will probably not do so. The best response is to strengthen fundamentals, notably economic flexibility and dynamism, together with energy resilience. In this context, as the WEO notes, it is essential to make support for people vulnerable to shocks targeted and temporary.

The time for throwing public money around freely has come to an end. It would help if the shocks stopped, too. Alas, given our leaders, I would not bet on that. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>jxfzsy<![CDATA[Kenmare Resources lowers production forecast as it continues talks with Abu Dhabi suitor]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/15/kenmare-lowers-production-forecast-as-it-continues-talks-with-abu-dhabi-suitor/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/15/kenmare-lowers-production-forecast-as-it-continues-talks-with-abu-dhabi-suitor/Thu, 15 Oct 2026 11:57:16 +0000Kenmare Resources, the Dublin-listed titanium minerals miner, has lowered the full-year production forecast for its most important product as it continues takeover talks with a company ultimately controlled by the Abu Dhabi royal family.

The company said on Thursday it now expected to produce 710,000-750,000 tonnes of ilmenite, which is used in the manufacture of everything from paints to plastics and textiles, at its Moma mine in Mozambique, southern Africa, this year. It previously targeted about 800,000 tonnes.

Ilmenite production fell 17 per cent last year to 842,300 tonnes.

Kenmare said the forecast downgrade was a result of “continuing commissioning challenges” at its recently upgraded largest mining plant, known as WCP A, which the group is moving to its largest ore zone, Nataka. Nataka contains about 70 per cent of Moma’s nine billion tonnes of mineral resources, according to the company.

Ilmenite is now well into its fourth year of price decline – driven by Chinese producers, operating at home and in Africa, continuing to oversupply the market. However, Kenmare said its average price for the product rose during the third quarter as it sold more “higher value” ilmenite product.

It said the price of zircon, which accounts for about a quarter of Kenmare revenues and is used to make ceramic tiles, is continuing to improve, having stabilised and started to rise last year.

Chief executive Tom Hickey said the company was continuing to “engage constructively” with the government of Mozambique over a new Moma production and exports royalty agreement and “remains focused on bringing these discussions to a positive conclusion in the near-term”.

The previous 20-year accord expired just before the end of 2024, though the terms were to remain in place until a new one was reached.

The Irish Times reported last week on how Kenmare Resources had attracted bid interest from Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding (IRH). Kenmare subsequently confirmed it had received a non-binding proposal from IRH, which has been given a deadline to announce at least a firm intention to make a formal bid by 5pm on November 17th.

IRH is a unit of International Holding Company, which is chaired by sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the United Arab Emirates deputy ruler and overseer of the business interests of Abu Dhabi’s ruling Al Nahyan family.

Shares in Kenmare are up about 25 per cent since news of the bid approach. However, they remain down almost 20 per cent from the level at which they were changing hands a year ago.

]]><![CDATA[Aryzta shares rally on appointment of bakery veteran as chairman]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/15/aryzta-shares-rally-on-appointment-of-bakery-veteran-as-chairman/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/15/aryzta-shares-rally-on-appointment-of-bakery-veteran-as-chairman/Thu, 15 Oct 2026 10:53:44 +0000Aryzta shares rallied on Thursday as the maker of par-baked breads and pastries cleared up governance questions by deciding to promote its lead independent director, German bakery veteran Heiner Kamps, as chairman at its next annual general meeting (AGM) in May.

The Zurich-listed group, formed in 2008 through the merger of Dublin-based IAWS and Swiss bakery group Hiestand, confirmed that current chairman and interim chief executive Urs Jordi will become permanent chief executive following the AGM next year.

Shares in Aryzta, owner of the Cuisine de France brand in the Republic, rose as much as 5.4 per cent. However, they remain down by more than a fifth so far this year amid declining sales in Europe, led by Germany, its largest market, as consumers have become more price-sensitive.

Jordi was installed as chairman in late 2020 following a boardroom coup and held a dual chairman-chief executive role for several years – against Swiss codes of best corporate governance practice – as he led a turnaround of the business.

Jordi became chairman early last year as Michael Schai, a former managing director of Aryzta’s Asia-Pacific region, became chief executive. However, he took on the additional role of interim chief executive in October after Schai quit after only nine months as the top executive.

“Aryzta has a strong position in the international bake-off market, and I see considerable potential for the business,” said Heiner. “As chairman, I want to focus on our strategic priorities and refresh the board to bring in new experience and perspectives.”

Heiner is best known for founding the Kamps bakery chain in Germany in 1982, before stepping down in 2002 following the sale of the business, which by then had more than 1,000 stores, to Italian food group Barilla. He has also previously served as chief executive of fast-food chain Nordsee and dairy processor Müller Group.

He and Jordi were two of three candidates installed as Aryzta directors at an extraordinary general meeting in September 2020 after rebel shareholders, led by Swiss investor Veraison, secured backing from voters for a boardroom overhaul. The company’s three former Irish directors, including chairman Gary McGann, as well as one Swiss board member, signalled they were stepping down before the meeting.

Aryzta’s sales fall more than 2% to €1.06bn, new results show

Aryzta saw its centre of gravity move from Ireland to Switzerland following a boardroom shake-up.

Jordi’s reboot has included the sale of unwanted assets, including Aryzta’s former problem North American business and Brazilian unit, reduction of debt and a greater focus on innovation in baked products.

The group said in August, as it unveiled a weak set of results for the first half of the year, that it was “reviewing all options for Germany to maximise shareholder value”. It confirmed on Thursday that it would reveal its plans for that market when it issues a trading update on October 26th.

]]>Nick Bradshaw for The Irish Times

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445269/">
   <title>Onlinewerbung als Einfallstor für Spionage</title>
   <description>Forschende des Citizen Lab von der Universität Toronto haben dokumentiert, wie manipulierte Onlinewerbung dazu genutzt werden kann, Endgeräte wie Computer und Handys unbemerkt mit Spionagesoftware zu infizieren, ohne dass die Opfer je einen Klick machen müssen. Laut einer am Donnerstag veröffentlichten Studie steht dabei die israelische Werbefirma Discover-Tech im Fokus. Die Anzeigen wurden auch auf Geräten in Netzwerken von Regierungen und internationaler Organisationen ausgespielt. Experten sehen dringenden Regulierungsbedarf im Onlinewerbemarkt.</description>
   <link>https://orf.at/stories/3445269/</link>
   <dc:subject>IT</dc:subject>
