Poland’s interior ministry has withdrawn a proposal to make it a criminal offence, punishable by up to three years in prison, to provide support to migrants who are in the country illegally. The idea had prompted criticism from human rights groups and even opposition from within the government.

The interior ministry said the amendment had been intended to clamp down on migrant smuggling. But activists feared it would criminalise humanitarian aid, such as that provided to migrants who have irregularly crossed the border from Belarus.

Za udzielenie bezinteresownej pomocy migrantom nie będzie groziła kara do trzech lat więzienia. Po burzy, którą wywołała publikacja „Rzeczpospolitej” i po sprzeciwie resortu rodziny, MSWiA wycofuje się z pomysłu „karania za podanie posiłku”.https://t.co/Q0N52IMRVn

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 15, 2026

Under current Polish law, anyone who facilitates the illegal stay of a person in Poland in exchange for financial or personal benefit can be jailed for up to five years.

However, this week, the interior ministry proposed an amendment that would also have penalised anyone who knowingly “enabled or facilitated” the illegal stay of someone in Poland, even if not for financial or personal benefit. The offence would have been punishable by up to three years in prison.

“Currently, this behaviour is not criminalised, creating a loophole for those who exploit such situations and, under the pretext of helping migrants, aid them in their illegal stay, thus serving as a springboard for further illegal migration,” wrote deputy interior minister Czesław Mroczek, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily.

 

That immediately prompted concern that the law could be used against volunteers and residents of border areas who provide aid – such as food, water, medical treatment, clothing or shelter – to migrants who have crossed illegally from Belarus.

Since 2021, tens of thousands of people, mainly from Asia and Africa, have tried to cross that border with the encouragement and support of the Belarusian authorities. They have sometimes used violence against Polish border officers.

Poland and the EU accuse Belarus of “weaponising” migration as part of the “hybrid warfare” being waged by Russia and its allies against European countries. They have implemented tough border protection measures to prevent crossings and facilitate “pushbacks” of those who cross.

However, many human rights and aid organisations argue that the migrants – over 100 of whom have died around the border since 2021 – are often victims of this process and need humanitarian support.

Two dead bodies found in the river on Poland's border with Belarus likely belong to migrants from a group seen being pushed into the water by Belarusian officers as part of efforts to encourage irregular crossings into the EU, says a Polish minister https://t.co/xsnPd6FeO3

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2025

In response to the interior ministry’s proposal, 61 organisations, including Amnesty International, the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and the Auschwitz-Birkenau Foundation, signed a joint statement condemning the plans, which they said “violate international standards binding Poland”.

The organisations warned that the proposed wording could expose medical staff treating migrants, lawyers providing legal assistance, facilities working with children, and organisations supporting victims of human trafficking to criminal liability.

“This measure is not aimed at smugglers, but rather at activists or residents of border areas who provide humanitarian aid to foreign nationals who have crossed the border illegally and are present in Poland,” attorney Radosław Baszuk told the Rzeczpospolita daily.

Baszuk previously represented five Polish activists who were prosecuted for providing food, clothing and shelter to a group of Middle Eastern migrants who had entered Poland from Belarus in 2022.

A group of five activists have been found not guilty of enabling the illegal presence in Poland of Middle Eastern migrants whom they provided aid to after they had irregularly crossed the border from Belarus.

Prosecutors had been seeking prison sentences https://t.co/RpfhVWL4hY

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 8, 2025

They were acquitted last year, with the ruling made final in March this year after an appeal. But Baszuk told Rzeczpospolita that, under the interior ministry’s proposed amendment to the relevant law, his clients could been convicted.

On Wednesday, Poland’s commissioner for human rights, Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram, also wrote to the justice ministry to “express concern” that the proposed changes “could lead to criminal liability for charitable or humanitarian activities undertaken towards individuals whose residence status has not yet been regulated”.

Even a member of the government, the minister for family, labour and social policy, Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk, expressed her “firm opposition” to the plans on social media. She is from The Left (Lewica), one of the junior partners in Poland’s ruling coalition.

By Daniel Tilles

Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called.

Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign.

When will the election take place?

Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023.

Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible).

It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term.

How does voting work?

The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list).

The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat.

How is a government formed?

A government can only be formed if it can win a vote of confidence in the Sejm.

After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence.

If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm.

Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister.

That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023

If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. However, whereas the previous two votes require an absolute majority (większość bezwzględna) to be carried, this time only a simple majority is needed, making it easier to form a minority government.

If this third and final attempt does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called.

Who is likely to form the next government?

At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture.

According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%.

Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%.

Rolling 30-day average support in polls for Poland’s main political parties (source: eWybory.eu)

If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition.

It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun.

However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside.

The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law.

 

There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government.

PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult.

All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation.

What about the Senate?

The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset.

It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO).

In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026

The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies.

In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition.

To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023.

What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest.

What role will Nawrocki play in all of this?

Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work.

Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition.

During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right.

However, the extent to which he will be involved in the election campaign is unclear. Some figures on the right hope that Nawrocki will act as a figurehead, using his positive relations with parties across the right-wing opposition to bring them together.

Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition.

What issues are likely to feature in the campaign?

A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer.

Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. If Washington confirms that the base will go ahead, Nawrocki will seek to take the credit, based on his good relationship with Trump.

On this point, though, it is worth noting the split within the opposition. While PiS and Rozwój Plus are strongly pro-American, Confederation and, to an even greater extent, KKP, are opposed to a greater US presence in Poland.

In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march.

Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall.

His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city.

Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people.

In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”.

However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”.

“I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.”

Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments.

 

Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch).

During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed.

When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would.

However, he added that he was doing this as a “legalist” who respects the current legal situation. “If a different political party wins [parliamentary elections] next year and changes the law in Poland, it [recognition of foreign same-sex marriages] won’t happen,” he told Radio Kraków.

In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union.

The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries.

Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue.

Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46).

The standoff between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president.

Berek is now the fifth judge to take their oath without presidential approval. The previous four have been denied entry to the TK, and speculation is rife that the government may soon take action to ensure that the excluded judges are able to take up their positions.

PILNE 🚨 dr Maciej Berek złożył w Sejmie ślubowanie na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego! pic.twitter.com/sZlzLnsL3M

Under Polish law, a new TK judge must swear an oath “before the president”. However, since Berek was elected to the TK by the government’s majority in parliament in early September, Nawrocki has refused to swear him in.

The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so.

Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge.

Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge.

 

With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present.

The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK.

The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present.

The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding.

Later on Monday, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, confirmed that Poland believes the attack was carried out “on behalf of the Russian security services”.

 

The incident in question took place on 23 September at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which has relied heavily on Starlink connections since Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Firefighters were called out that evening to a fire at the facility, which is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel. The next day, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gakowski revealed that the blaze had been started deliberately and “the modus operandi is clearly Russian”.

Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe. Those have included a series of arson attacks, including one that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and another at a drone factory that is used to supply the Ukrainian military.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Fri, 16 Oct 2026 17:50:08 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 These are the best literary hotels in Europe https://www.cityam.com/these-are-the-best-literary-hotels-in-europe/ Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:08:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2466510

Poet, playwright and screenwriter Alexandra Pereira on her favourite literary hotels. Where will you check in to pen your tome? If you’re looking for inspiration for isolation, here’s where to book a room of one’s own, just a short train or flight from London, as well as the renowned, and sometimes controversial writers from the [...]]]>

Poet, playwright and screenwriter Alexandra Pereira on her favourite literary hotels. Where will you check in to pen your tome?

If you’re looking for inspiration for isolation, here’s where to book a room of one’s own, just a short train or flight from London, as well as the renowned, and sometimes controversial writers from the destinations.

The best literary hotels

Maison Proust, Paris
In the spirit of: Marcel Proust, Edouard Louis
Womblike quarters in rich and devouring Belle Epoque style. With bedrooms decorated in rich colourways such as royal blue and gold, with sumptuous upholstery, shutters and heavy curtains, the feel here is about nesting and restoring before heading out onto the nearby streets of Le Marais.

The library of Proust relics next to the excellent bar is a great spot for reading and writing, while the below ground La Mer spa features a pool and a star covered ceiling that makes the room feel like a grandiose sensory deprivation tank.
Go to maison-proust.com

Wilmina, Berlin
In the spirit of: Christopher Isherwood, Hermann Hesse
Austere yet light-filled, this was once a courthouse, then a women‘s prison and has been reimagined as a hotel with rooftop pool and sauna. Desks are long and natural sunlight pours into every room.

Its Charlottenburg (my favourite Berlin neighbourhood) location makes for quiet rest and excellent people watching, free from the party crowds. Lovis is a lovely restaurant and their in-house bakery is gorgeous. Their Amtsalon art and cultural space is great for quiet reading or working, and also hosts events.
Go to wilmina.com

Monastero Santa Rosa, Amalfi Coast
In the spirit of: Pier Paolo Pasolini, Virginia Woolf
Where better to sequester oneself and those novel notes than the village of Conca dei Marini? Here there is one of the very best literary hotels. Along the Amalfi coast you’ll find a heady mix of crowds and delicately quiet spots, as the palazzos and monasteries of variously storied towns peer down from grand cliffs over the blue waters. There’s nothing quite like the pared back majesty of an ecclesiastical space that helps one centre and let ideas flow.

Delightfully true to its origins, rooms are airy and simply comfortable, while the terraces, balconettes and dining rooms are quintessentially Amalfi: part opulent, part quaint. Their tasting menu journeys across Campania, and can be made deliciously vegetarian too. Historically, the sisters who once ran this monastery contributed in many ways to the local community including as an apothecary – and designing and funding an aqueduct from Mount Vocito to Piazza Olmo to provide water for locals.
Go to monasterosantarosa.com

Read more: The Amalfi Coast is at its best in October – here’s why

Literary hotels: write love letters a la Casanova

Ca’ Di Dio, Venice
In the spirit of: Ruzzante, Giacomo Casanova
It might not be de rigeur to swim in the Venetian canals but gazing out onto them is plenty rewarding. This is probably my favourite Venice stay as it’s a little quieter and less full of gilt and drapery than some of the more known palazzos.

Still, its ceilings are grand, the light is beautiful, rooms are spacious and quiet for working, with lots of clean lines and quietly luxurious materials, and the huge sell is its peaceful garden courtyard with swing chairs, tables and an excellent restaurant. The fresh pasta and raw lagoon fish dishes are to die, breakfast serves bubbles, plus the hotel arranges private boat tours out to Murano to watch glass blowing artisans in action. Channel one of the region’s earliest playwrights, Ruzzante, or better yet, write love letters a la Casanova from your suite.
Go to vretreats.com

The Dolli, Athens
In the spirit of: Yanis Varoufakis, Alexandra K*
A lot of Athens boutiques struggle to capture the essence of the classics whilst exercising a contemporary glamour. The Dolli nails it, with a dream collection of Greek and Egyptian antiquities and Cocteau, through to Michael McDonagh and Les Lalanne. The rooftop pool and restaurant has breathtaking panoramic views of the Acropolis and the Parthenon, and monuments like the Ancient Agora, the Erechtheion, and the classical buildings of Plaka.

Rooms are chicly mapped out with high ceilings, secret wardrobes, rainforest showers and in-house wine. The decor is clean girl aesthetic with splashes of antiquity and Frieze – a spirited place from which to write. The pastries and sweets in the lobby make you feel like you’re in Alice in Wonderland.
Go to thedolli.com

Dua Lipa’s favourite place to stay

Hotel Valldemossa, Mallorca
In the spirit of: Aurore Dupin (George Sand)
Cracking open the shutters and overlooking the valleys and mountains surrounding the magical town of Valldemossa, with a faint baa of sheep drifting into the window, I’ve never been happier to pitch up and work on some writing. You can wander down to the pools or spa room (where a masseuse named Love will pummel all your stresses away), the outdoor gym, or have a bite to eat at the Japanese-Peruvian restaurant (excellent). But being private and hidden away here is very easy – and the hikes, biking trails and local eateries provide more than enough slow-life respite from the desk.
Go to valldemossahotel.com

Hotel D’Angleterre, Copenhagen
In the spirit of: Hans Christian Andersen
It’s said that the famed fairytale author HC Andersen holed up at this Danish institution when his own apartment down at Nyhavn set alight. Now, this is also Dua Lipa’s fave place to stay, and with its huge loft suites overlooking Kongens Nytorv, perfect French restaurant, you can see why the greats decamped here – a lot of natural light pools into the dining areas and suites, creating optimum conditions for writing, plus many of the city’s greatest delights surround the building, from all night watering holes to Michelin starred restaurants – and a lot of boats and sailors. The hotel also now has an underground spa that’s gorgeously quiet and dimly lit.
Go to dangleterre.com

Pride without prejudice: the best literary hotels

Artist Residence, Bristol
In the spirit of: Sarah Kane
On the corner of a verdant town square that’s spitting distance from some of the city’s best galleries, pubs, cafes and wine bars – as well as vintage shops galore – this hotel feels part curator’s home, part co-working space/library, and part bar/restaurants and locals’ hang out.

The best rooms overlook the square, with huge Georgian windows letting the light spill onto massive tables ideal for working. The main suite even has an in-room roll top tub so deep you can almost swim (details such as walk-in shower, stripped floors and local art also sing). Friday’s happy hour is an impressive, inclusive calendar of talks, screenings and more make the place feel like you’re a true artist in residence.
Go to artistresidence.co.uk

The Gainsborough, Bath
In the spirit of: Jane Austen
With the city’s only hotel access to the spa waters, this is pretty much the only place for any Janeite or spa fetishist. The recently renovated suites are sumptuous places to retreat after a scrub and massage in the spa (using all natural products) and a dip in the healing waters. Wifi is fast and views across the golden Bathstone exteriors of the city’s marvellous architecture make for a sublime place to channel your own writerly pride without prejudice.
Go to thegainsboroughbathspa.co.uk

]]> 2466510Alexandra Pereira Alexandra Pereira Was the transfer window impacted by UK tax rules? https://www.cityam.com/was-the-transfer-window-impacted-by-uk-tax-rules/ Sat, 17 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2466365

This summer’s transfer window again showed the purchasing power of the Premier League, with almost £3.5bn being spent on transfer fees. And, while there were players being bought from foreign teams, there was also a significant number of very high value transfers between Premier League clubs this summer, which is notable compared to previous transfer [...]]]>

This summer’s transfer window again showed the purchasing power of the Premier League, with almost £3.5bn being spent on transfer fees. And, while there were players being bought from foreign teams, there was also a significant number of very high value transfers between Premier League clubs this summer, which is notable compared to previous transfer windows.

Given the Manchester City case, most people are now aware of the Premier League’s profit and sustainability rules (PSR), and it is clear that these have been relevant for recruitment at club level. However, could the abolition of the Remittance Basis in April 2025 have dissuaded overseas-based players from making the move to the UK?

Old tax rules

Previously, players at the top teams who played games in Europe could claim relief on those games under the Overseas Workday Relief (OWR) regime. As an example, if a player plays 10 per cent of their games overseas, then they could exempt 10 per cent of their salary from UK tax for the first three tax years (subject to certain conditions).

They also had a period of up to 15 years where non-UK income and gains (outside of their salary) could be sheltered from UK tax under the Remittance Basis, as long as these were not brought to the UK.

New regime

However, the new Foreign Income and Gains (or FIG) regime has rung in important changes since being introduced from 6 April 2025.

This regime provides a full exemption on non-UK income and gains, which is more generous than the Remittance Basis. However, the FIG regime is only available for four tax years which, given the way the transfer windows fall, would likely only last a player for three seasons.

While the period that OWR can be claimed has been extended to four tax years (from three), this is limited to a total amount of £300,000 per year. This is a significant sum for most people, but for players at the top teams who are earning in excess of this amount a week, it severely weakens the appeal of this relief.

Impact on players

The impact of these new rules means that there is a potentially more generous regime available for those who would not benefit from OWR, however for a much shorter period.

As such, for a player who may already have built significant wealth from their playing career, the FIG regime does not provide the mid-term tax benefits that the Remittance Basis afforded. For footballers, having consistency with their tax position is extremely important, especially as they only have a relatively short career to earn these levels of income.

This surely is a consideration for non-UK players when considering offers from the Premier League compared to, say, renegotiating a deal at their existing club.

Also, given that players who are currently playing in England are already caught by the UK tax system, is this a consideration for clubs looking to buy from other Premier League teams? 

It is not a stretch to think that a newly recruited footballer from outside the UK will have an eye on the end of the FIG regime and be looking to move abroad after three seasons in the UK.

At the same time, we have also seen a rise in British players moving abroad, including to countries with attractive tax regimes such as Saudi Arabia and Italy.

While I don’t think there will be much public sympathy for highly paid footballers in the lead up to the Budget, could we see a relaxation of the recently introduced rules to keep the Premier League as the global force it has grown into, especially given the negative attention of the recent Manchester City case?

Adam Jefferies is a director at PKF Littlejohn.

The Post Office is weighing a bid for one of the UK’s largest independent ATM operators in a move that would expand its cashpoint empire, City AM can reveal. The group, which facilitates the largest branch-based access-to-cash network in the United Kingdom, is exploring a deal for Notemachine after it was put up for sale [...]]]>

The Post Office is weighing a bid for one of the UK’s largest independent ATM operators in a move that would expand its cashpoint empire, City AM can reveal.

The group, which facilitates the largest branch-based access-to-cash network in the United Kingdom, is exploring a deal for Notemachine after it was put up for sale its by parent company, Brink’s, sources said. 

The Brink’s Company bought Notemachine in October 2022 for nearly $180m. The firm is one of the largest independent ATM providers in the UK, operating thousands of cash machines and supplying around 20 per cent of all cash dispensed across the country.

A potential deal would complement the Post Office’s banking hub model, which seeks to replace closed bank branches. It would allow the group to move beyond its brick-and-mortar store fronts and rapidly deploy community banking offerings in rural and high-traffic areas.

Over 30 banks and building societies pay a multi-million pound annual fee to the Post Office for network access, which allows millions of customers to use services at its sites. 

Beauty parade underway after Brink’s deal

Lenders partnered with the Post Office in 2017 for “The Banking Framework”, and extended the collaboration for three-years in 2022. Last year, a new five-year deal was agreed to keep cash services running on the high street.

Brink’s – which specialises in cash and valuables management – announced a mega-deal to acquire global fintech firm NCR Atleos earlier this year for $6.6bn. 

The deal was flagged by the UK’s competition watchdog, which warned a merger of the two entities would reduce ATM choices for businesses and potentially lead to higher fees for consumers accessing cash.

Brink’s said it would divest its ATM units in order to land the greenlight for the merger. In early October, the firm said the Competition Markets Authority had accepted the “proposed remedy” and it was engaging with potential suitors.

The Post Office and Brink’s declined to comment.

An Omaze spokesperson told City AM the platform “has been paying VAT in the UK since 2021.” Omaze lists itself on its website as “not a charity raffle, house or cash raffle [...]]]>

Luxury house prize draw platform Omaze has appealed against HMRC over whether paid entries in its prize draws are subject to standard-rate VAT.

An Omaze spokesperson told City AM the platform “has been paying VAT in the UK since 2021.”

Omaze lists itself on its website as “not a charity raffle, house or cash raffle or house or cash lottery but a prize draw”.

An organisation that offers a free entry route to a draw, such as a postcard option, avoids being regulated as a lottery under the Gambling Act, and HMRC categorises the service as a prize draw, meaning its paid entries do not qualify for the VAT exemption that regulated lotteries receive.

However, earlier this year, Labour MP Dan Tomlinson, who was responsible for HMRC and tax policy until July, confirmed that prize draws offering both paid and free entry routes “are not eligible for VAT exemption and paid entries will be subject to VAT at the standard rate of 20 per cent.”

This landmark dispute went to the First Tier Tax Tribunal, which heard the appeal on Friday, with a decision expected in Spring next year.

Appeal ‘seeks clarity and consistency’ for industry

Since launching in the UK in 2020, after being founded in the US in 2012, Omaze has run prize draws where entrants can win multi-million-pound houses, cars, or money for a relatively small fee. The houses are located across the UK, with many in desirable areas such as the Cotswolds and Cornwall.

The fundraising platform donates a proportion of the draw proceeds to a charity, and guarantees a minimum donation of £1m to its partner charities with each draw.

“Our appeal seeks clarity and consistency in how VAT applies across the prize draw industry. Omaze has raised more than £150m for UK charities, yet is one of the few prize draw operators HMRC has required to pay VAT on sales. As it would for any business in any sector, this disparity affects our ability to operate sustainably,” an Omaze spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added: “It also affects our ability to continue raising significant funds for good causes. Having sought to resolve the issue for several years, we are pursuing this appeal to establish a level playing field. We appreciate the court’s attention to this issue.”

It was, in the immortal, viral words of former Manchester United footballer Gary Neville, “the banker”. It was “the no-brainer – the one that couldn’t fail, the one that’s never failed”.

The England right-back was talking about his former club’s 2016 decision to appoint Jose Mourinho as head coach. The Portuguese firebrand would, top brass had hoped, put right a years-long spell of underperformance and vanquish the ghost of their totemic manager, Sir Alex Ferguson, once and for all. In the end, though, it wasn’t to be, and after just two and a half years in charge – with no league titles to show for it – Mourinho was given his marching orders.

But Neville’s remarks could – with a bit of imagination – just as easily apply to the frenzied speculation in the run-up to this month’s Budget.

Unlike his kite-flying, pitch-rolling predecessor, John Healey has remained notably tight-lipped on the composition of his maiden fiscal event. What little information industrious reporters have teased out of the Treasury has been patchwork-like and bit-part, leaving captains of industry, investors and even lobbyists firmly in the dark.

But the one tax hike that has looked nailed on ever since the Rotherham MP named the date of his Budget – the “banker”, if you will – has been a windfall tax of one form or another on the City’s eminent banking sector.

If reports out last night are to be believed, that “no brainer” bet that Labour will squeeze billions of pounds out of the UK’s lenders is starting to pay out. Healey is still, says The Guardian, weighing his options. One move under consideration is to reverse Jeremy Hunt’s reduction of the bank surcharge. Also rumoured is an overhaul of the way the Treasury treats the Bank of England’s interest payments on commercial bank reserves. But where and how the axe falls is just window dressing. The reality is: the banks are going to get it.

Lobbying efforts come up short

It is – despite an intensive and relentless rearguard action from banking execs – a fate to which many in the sector were resigned. High street lenders and their investment counterparts have, for the best part of three years now, been churning out record profits off the back of consecutive geopolitical shocks that have kept interest rates higher for longer. The industry was also on the chopping block at both of Rachel Reeves’ ill-fated fiscal events, before the former Chancellor eventually yielded to their warnings that a windfall tax would impact her “number-one mission” to grow the economy.

In his first few months in No. 11, Healey, however, has appeared far less concerned with trifling matters like ‘growth’ and ‘prosperity’. And after squeezing other parts of the business ecosystem at other tax-raising Budgets (carried interest was raised in 2024, employer Nics mostly impacted low-skilled industries and business rates hit those with a heavy bricks and mortar presence), a sense of foreboding had spread through Canary Wharf and the Square Mile.

As a result, lenders’ shares have not moved as much as you might think this morning. The two most susceptible to the whims of UK lawmakers – Lloyds and Natwest – are down just 2.1 and 2.0 per cent respectively. Meanwhile HSBC and Standard Chartered, which boast a far more international footprint, are actually in the green.

But just because every man and their dog expected Healey to go after banks’ profits, does not make it good policy. As the chart above shows, lenders in Blighty are taxed the most of any major European finance hub – a fact that JP Morgan’s Jamie Dimon has said, obviously, plays into investment and expansion decisions. And – as the sector’s indefatigable industry bodies have warned – it will also eat into the price and volumes loans banks can afford to issue to capital-starved SMEs, choking off growth in the engine room of the UK economy.

Above all, though, is what it signifies about the mindset that UK policymakers increasingly have towards the success of cyclical businesses. Are you an energy company doing well because of unusually high oil prices? Expect a windfall tax. Are you an airline pumping out profits because of the opposite? What’s not to say there might be one coming down the line for you too?

When Manchester United made the widely expected decision to fire Jose Mourinho in 2018, it did so after he had won the Europa League and League Cup, and secured second place in the Premier League. In the eight years since, the once-great football dynasty has given its fans just one trophy to celebrate and is currently 13th in the league. As in the case of Gary Neville’s former club, Healey’s approach to Britain’s banking industry, risks being less “no-brainer” and more hare-brained.

    New inheritance tax rules will drastically alter how people use their pensions, and put a lot of individuals in difficult positions, writes Steve Gauke

    For years, pensions have been one of the most effective ways for families to pass wealth to the next generation. But from April 2027, that will change, with most unused pension funds being brought into the scope of inheritance tax.

    The problem isn’t simply that more families will face an inheritance tax bill. It’s that many may not realise they’re affected until it’s too late to prepare. We risk sleepwalking into a situation where thousands of families face unexpected tax liabilities at an already difficult time. Many families have planned around the old legislation, leaving a potential knowledge gap between the government distributing the new rules and the families who must understand them.

    The scale of the change is significant; the government’s estimates suggest that around 10,500 estates will pay inheritance tax for the first time in 2027 to 2028, and that a further 38,500 will pay more, with the average bill expected to rise by around £34,000. These are, of course, only estimates, but the changes will drastically alter how people use their pensions in response. This shift will put a lot of individuals in difficult positions, after all, behind every one of those figures is a family who will be asked to find a large sum of money at a very difficult time.     NIMBYs and rising migration have both been blamed for the UK’s housing shortage. What’s the actual problem, asks Ben Hopkinson

    It is clear that the UK does not have enough homes for its population. There are two stories about why this has happened. The first, told by YIMBYs, is that it is simply too hard to build homes and expand the housing supply. The other, told by migration hawks, is that the record numbers entering Britain have driven up demand for scarce properties. Both have a truth to them, and action solely on one is not enough to end the housing crisis. 

    How bad is the UK’s housing shortage?

    Of all the major Western European countries, the UK has the second fewest homes per 1,000 people. To catch up to the average, the UK needs 6.9m more homes. This number has grown from 6.5m homes using 2023 data, as net migration has outpaced our ability to build homes, which isn’t true for most other European countries. England accounts for 6.2m of those missing homes.

    Historically, the UK, and especially England, has not built enough homes. Since the early 1980s, France has grown its housing stock by an average of 1.07 per cent a year, while England has only managed 0.82 per cent a year. This may seem like a small difference, but it adds up after four decades of compounding.

    England has averaged only 178,000 homes a year. Matching France’s housing stock growth would require building 246,000 homes a year. Achieving the government’s 300,000 home a year target would be useful for helping to close the gap. Sadly it is almost certain to be missed, with even Angela Rayner, the re-appointed housing secretary, conceding the manifesto commitment was actually a ‘stretch target’.

    Had England matched France’s building rate since the early 1980s, it would have 2.9m additional homes. This alone would have been enough to close half of England’s housing shortage. 

    Every single year, France has expanded its housing stock faster than its population has grown. England cannot say the same. After barely rising from the mid-2000s, England’s homes per 1,000 peaked in 2021. Since then, high levels of migration have reduced this number. This means that the housing shortage is getting worse despite 1.1m homes being built since 2020.

    This is where the migration hawk story comes in, with claims that large-scale migration has driven up demand for our paltry supply of homes. 

    Has migration contributed?

    Had net migration been capped at 100,000 a year since 1997, and the rate of housebuilding remained unchanged, England would now have 473 homes per 1,000. That makes up about a third of the gap that England has with the rest of Western Europe.

    The recent spike of migration has given further credence to the demand-side story. Had net migration stayed in the tens of thousands since 2020 instead of the record-breaking wave, house prices would be roughly £15,270, or 5.2 per cent, lower in England. This spike in migration could be the missing puzzle piece that explains why high interest rates have not had the catastrophic impact on house prices that many predicted.

    So where do these two stories leave us? Building an achievable number of homes could have closed half the gap, while keeping to the oft-made manifesto pledge of tens of thousands not hundreds of thousands of net migrants would have closed a third of the gap. Both help explain why there are so few homes per capita in the UK. Combined, they would have come close to ending the housing shortage. 

    The mismatch between high demand and low supply drives many of the symptoms of the housing crisis: the unaffordability of properties, smaller and lower quality homes, and the young being priced out of home ownership. 

    We don’t have a time machine to change the policy decisions made decades ago that have caused the housing crisis. But the policy choices taken today and after the next general election will decide whether we make progress in closing our housing shortage or allow it to grow even more.

    Tens of thousands of taxpayers were handed money back from HMRC last year after savers had too much tax deducted from their pension withdrawals, City AM can reveal.

    HMRC processed 54,166 pension withdrawal repayments in the 2025/26 financial year, worth around £188m, according to figures obtained through a Freedom of Information request.

    During the financial year, HMRC received 107,880 repayment claim forms. On average, impacted savers were repaid roughly £3,470.

    The overtaxation by the department stemmed from default Pay As You Earn (PAYE) rules used to collect income tax. The PAYE system is the government’s primary method for collecting income tax, national insurance and student loan payments directly from an employee’s wage slip.

    It also deducts taxes from private or workplace pension withdrawals. Under current rules Brits can access their pension pot from age 55, with 25 per cent of the total value of the pot taken tax-free.

    But in some circumstances, a single withdrawal can be treated as monthly income, as pension providers rarely hold an up-to-date tax code for customers, leading HMRC to tax the withdrawal as though it were regular income.

    Savers must apply for money back instead of HMRC issuing an automatic refund.

    Steve Webb, partner at pensions consultant LCP and former pensions minister, described the need to file a form to recover the money as “absurd” and an unnecessary burden for the department and taxpayers.

    “The whole system of overtaxing people on pension withdrawals and expecting them to fill in one of three different claim forms to get their tax back is absurd…. a huge waste of taxpayer time and effort,” he said.

    “For most people, the right answer will turn out to be that they need to have basic rate tax deducted at source and that should be what happens. For people who turn out to have been higher rate taxpayers at the end of the year it is a simple matter to collect the rest through the end year assessment process. This system is run purely for the convenience of HMRC rather than the taxpayer and is long overdue for reform.”

    ‘Waste of taxpayer time’

    The vast majority of refunded money was claimed through P55 forms, which covers partial withdrawals, with £124.5m returned across 37,116 claims.

    Brits who filled in P53Z forms, used by people who have completely wiped out their retirement pot but can still rely on other income, had £51.8m paid out from 14,372 claims. Meanwhile, an additional £10.8m was refunded across 2,519 P50Z form claims, which covers those who have no other existing income. 

    Nearly 160 claimants also used niche defined benefit forms in a bid to get money back, including P55DB, P53ZDB and P502DB. In total, savers who filed for a refund using these forms received around £0.85m.

    HMRC noted that it works through every case and does not reject claims, but not all applicants receive a payout, with only roughly half of the claims resulting in repayment.

    HMRC said: “This depends entirely on their personal circumstances…whether this is an underpayment for a previous year, if they have ongoing employment, and whether the pension has been taxed at the correct rate of tax.”

    Increasing awareness

    HMRC’s failure to immediately contact savers who were overtaxed means only those who spot the error and file a claim can attempt to get back their cash immediately.

    Others who do not identify the overcharge or choose not to submit a claim, typically have to wait until HMRC runs its end of financial year tax reconciliation process, meaning many often wait months for funds.

    HMRC said it could not provide the total number of people whose pension withdrawals had been overtaxed, or the total amount of tax over-deducted, without reviewing individual customer records.

    The findings come amid both HMRC and the Department of Work and Pensions (DWP) urging people to become more engaged with their pensions to prevent being overcharged and missing out on other financial benefits.

    According to statistics released by the DWP in May, the proportion of overpaid Pension Credit claims increased to 33 per cent in the 2025/26 tax year, up from 28 per cent the prior year.

    The two drivers behind incorrect payments were identified as claimants failing to fully declare their financial assets or spending time overseas that surpassed the limit that benefit rules permit. By April 2031, the government expects to save £370m.

    But despite the crackdown on Pension Credit claims, the benefit remains widely unclaimed by those who qualify for the payment.

    An HMRC spokesperson said: “Nobody ultimately overpays tax as a result of taking advantage of pension flexibility.

    “We will repay anyone who pays too much because they’re on an emergency tax code and individuals can claim a repayment earlier if they wish.”

    For much of the past decade and a half, describing the UK economy has been a relatively easy task. ‘Languid’ has often worked. ‘Stuttering’ has been another favourite. And when things have looked especially sullen, ‘moribund’ or ‘anaemic’ have more than sufficed.

    But if today’s GDP figures are anything to go by, then cliche-dependent hacks like this one might find themselves having to reach for their thesauruses in search of a new vernacular.

    Granted, a 0.1 per cent jump in economic activity in August is hardly cause to crack open the English sparkling wine. But it was, as almost every economist has been at pains to point out this morning, an expectation-defying 0.1 per cent nevertheless.

    The headwinds facing the upward nudge were manifold. And the sources of that resilience – improved productivity, early signs of a tech boom, and an uptick in our, yes, ‘moribund’ manufacturing sector – inspire some confidence.

    It is worth reflecting on why quite so many macro analysts are in such a celebratory mood. First, many had – quite understandably – expected the Middle East conflict, now stretching into its eighth month, to finally get its talons into business and consumer sentiment.

    Despite what Berenberg’s Andrew Wishart catchily frames as a “quadruple whammy” of rising taxes, higher energy prices, higher mortgage rates and a weak labour market, confidence has, in fact, been improving this year (albeit from a strikingly low ebb). And a look at consumer and services spending in today’s figures shows the trend has, again, defied expectations to the upside.

    Then there is the fact that August’s figure was going up against a tricky month-on-month comparative period. Boosted by spendthrift World Cup watchers, the UK economy grew by 0.4 per cent in both June and July, leading most economists to pencil in a minor contraction over the sleepier month of August.

    All of which means that over a three months, Britain’s once-languid economy has now grown by 0.7 per cent. It has also jumped 2.1 per cent over the past year, in what is our best 12 months since around 2017.

    “The UK’s resilience story continues,” Deutsche Bank’s Sanjay Raja said this morning. “It’s hard to overstate how strong the UK performance has been all year.”

    The UK economy’s bleak midwinter

    And yet, because we can’t have nice things, there is, I’m afraid, a ‘but’. And that ‘but’ relates to what comes after what most think will be a solid end to the year.

    Early forecasts suggest that the start of 2027 could look a lot different from much of 2026. The Bank of England is all but nailed on to raise interest rates at its next meeting in November, with another 25 basis-point hike expected in early 2027. That alone will considerably shift households’ breathing space – and with no end of the inflationary Iran war in sight – price pressure remains uncomfortably hot; especially with the economy chugging along as healthily as it is.

    Even more ominous is the direction of energy prices, which are due to build up a head of steam at the start of next year. By the Bank of England’s reckoning, households can expect their energy bills to jump by some 20 per cent in January. That, in turn, will help carry inflation to four per cent, double the monetary authority’s two per cent target. All the while, improvement in people’s pay is expected to slow.

    “The combination of rising inflation and slowing wage growth is a toxic mix for households’ real income growth,” says RSM UK’s Thomas Pugh.

    Then again, people much cleverer than me have been predicting a sharp economic downturn for much of this year – and it hasn’t materialised. But with so many competing headwinds, overwhelming consensus is we can only be so resilient. Journalists’ thesauruses appear safe… for now.

    Standing in the teeny tiny, Netflix-Christmas-film-coded courtyard outside Cloth Cornhill, I feel sad. This opening drills the final nail in the coffin of the former Simpsons Tavern, the capital’s oldest chophouse, which was on this site since 1757.

    Everyone’s got a story about whose fault it is that that chophouse closed. Rumours range from the former tenants being massively overdue rental payments before the pandemic, through to it being the greedy landlord’s fault. Either way, the former manager is bitter that in 2022, his run came to an end – he said this in a lengthy LinkedIn post – and rightly so: he was the final custodian of the Simpsons Tavern brand, which had been in place for 250 years.

    In the drizzle, my colleague and I spend 45 minutes admiring the expensive, shiny refurbishment. Nursing pints of ale, we discuss the whole sorry situation. Despite my empathy for the old guard, who still retain the rights to the Simpsons Tavern name and plan to open somewhere else in the “spirit” of Simpsons, it makes for tantalising gossip. I’d love to know what went down, but the landlord is uncontactable. It’s impossible not to feel that the fallout is one big shame. RIP Simpsons Tavern, for now, anyway.

    But today, we’re talking about Cloth Cornhill. Founders Ben Butterworth, Joe Haynes and Tom Hurst have recreated the old place as if it were 1757 again. The landlords were so scrupulous, they asked to see sample menus before they’d agree to hand over the keys, so this trio must be, at the very least, charismatic. Just don’t say that anything is in homage to the old venue or ‘bringing anything back’ as that gets them in murky legal waters.

    Cloth Cornhill: how about a ‘pie course’?

    Its gleaming mahogany high-backed benches have been buffered to within an inch of their lives, the pub reorganised so the feng shui is better – that’s a fancy way of saying it’s easier to get to the bar – and to give more emphasis to the building’s features, such as the front bay window. Period wooden floor replaces lino; two part-time workers spent six months polishing 22 faux vintage brass lamps.

    On autumn’s first sodden Monday, the place is heaving. If the brief was to recreate a cacophonous Dickensian tavern, consider that met. Only there are also quiet contemporary enhancements, such as sound dampening added to the ceiling so you can actually have a conversation. One lonely photo of a barmaid with two cakes in front of her boobs hangs upstairs as a reminder of the good old days. I’m told some of the waitresses used to show their breasts if they got tipped enough, and many from the Simpson’s Tavern days have returned after the reopening (I can’t promise they were the ones flashing the customers however).

    Former patrons have even demanded the old menu back. Is it pastiche? A little bit. How can it not be? But in 10 years, when the old guard have all died, no one will remember Simpsons Tavern anyway, they’ll just say there’s a really cool old school chophouse called Cloth Cornhill. Such is life.

    Prepare your gout stool

    As for the food, Victorian gentlemen would be preparing their gout stools. The menu features superlative spins on British comfort food. To kick off, devils on horseback (prunes filled with black pudding and wrapped in bacon) were just divine – dense enough to suck like boiled sweets. ‘Sausage on the side’ with mustard is delicious, the meat both course and smooth (a version of this dish was on the former Simpsons menu, although the owners insist it was inspired by a recipe in a book found during the refit).

    We are recommended the ‘pie course’, which is the most hedonistic thing I have ever heard. I decide on venison, bacon and prune, with pastry that was nine tenths butter, and it is obviously banging, a reflection of Hurst’s philosophy: locally sourced meat, diligently cooked and married with the odd unusual ingredient.

    We drink loads of booze to induce more hunger, plus we’re at Simpsons Tavern – sorry, Cloth Cornhill – and that’s what you do in here. “This place was known for gout production,” says our waiter, which I think was supposed to make us feel better about over-ordering. The sommelier brings over something from the Southern Rhone to follow a funky rose that tasted like overripe strawberries.

    Welsh rarebit – for dessert!

    From the mains, a stuffed potato dumpling with taleggio, girolles and saffron should surely be banned by the NHS. It is the sort of amped-up, 21st century comfort food that demonstrates how Hurst is future proofing the classics. It is the precursor to an enormous lamb chop, which was indecently tender, and served with anchovy butter. During our interview, the trio said they were proudly “countercultural” in their apathy towards healthy food, although the beetroot salad with hazelnut, goats curd and chicory is worth ordering.

    Dessert tries a little too hard to be modern. We had something chocolatey cut into a fancy shape, which was nice, but we really wanted spotted dick and sticky toffee pudding. Perhaps these felt too on the nose but please, boys, give the people what they want. Welsh rarebit – for dessert! – was more like it, doused in balsamic vinegar and served the way it always has been. The dippy, melted cheese popular from Simpsons Tavern, the waiter says, is off-menu but on hold for the old regulars.

    The house martini comes with sherry rather than vermouth, which is a nod to Haynes and Butterworth’s wine trading CV. It works, but mostly in ensuring I fall asleep in front of the TV with the light on when I get home. I’d briefly forgotten about feeling sad about Simpsons Tavern, which either makes me a sellout or Cloth Cornhill very good indeed – I’ll let you decide.

    An investigation by market intelligence platform Tussell found the government has awarded KPMG, Deloitte, EY and PwC over £1.5bn in contracts so far in 2026, more than the entirety of 2025, which stood at £1.04bn.

    The data showed it was the second most successful calendar year for the Big Four since Tussell began recording in 2012, beaten only by contracting during the height of the pandemic in 2020.

    Leading the Big Four, Deloitte secured £650m across 108 contracts this year. The bulk of these wins focused on IT services, digital transformation, and data analytics. Home Office IT spending accounted for the majority of this new work, including a standout £200m contract for Home Office Digital’s Data Services and Analytics (DSA) unit.

    KPMG and EY won the largest contract, worth £456m, awarded by the Cabinet Office, which covers training for civil servants over the next two years.

    In terms of rankings, despite being the smallest compared to its competitors, KPMG took second place, winning over £413m in government contract work. EY was third, with an overall value of £260m booked so far this year. Despite being the largest, PwC often takes a proportionally smaller share of public sector work than its rivals. It ranked fourth with over £211m.

    As the consultancy market tightens due to the influx of AI and private-sector pulling back on external spending due to an economic downturn, government work remains resilient for firms.

    Tamzen Isacsson, chief executive of the Management Consultancies Association (MCA), told City AM: “Consultants are playing a vital role in helping government improve public services for taxpayers, and their specialist expertise is in demand in areas such as digital transformation, cybersecurity, AI and organisational change.”

    Civil service skills gap challenge

    The increase in UK government spending comes after Labour pledged in 2024 to slash taxpayer spending on external consultants.

    The government unveiled plans for greater procurement control in November 2024, rolling out a framework to save £1.2bn by 2026 by freezing non-essential consultancy hires and targeting a 50 per cent spend reduction in the years to follow.

    However, the government’s biggest challenge is the civil service skills shortage, especially during digital transformation.

    Emma Carroll, principal consultant at Source Global Research, told City AM: “Often, consultants are brought in to tackle the most complex projects where specific expertise is needed and where there is a lack of internal talent, and there are some prime examples of this at play at the moment, including cybersecurity, technology implementation (including AI), or data readiness work, where the government simply can’t risk falling behind.

    “The defence sector has also been a critical area of focus for the UK government this year, and consulting support has been and will continue to be important here,” she added.

    Source predicts the UK public sector consulting market will grow by around five per cent in 2026, versus around six per cent for the wider consulting market.

    Isacsson added: “We recognise the fiscal pressures facing government and share its ambition to improve productivity and delivery across the public sector.     The Cabinet Office was contacted for comment.

    What’s one thing you love about the City of London?

    I love the mix of old and new. One minute you’re walking past St Paul’s and all that history, the next you’re looking up at a brand new building.

    And one thing you would change?

    I’m not sure it’s about changing something, but about making sure we don’t stand still. The UK has a fantastic position as a global financial centre, but maintaining that means embracing change, continuing to innovate and creating the right environment for businesses to grow.

    What’s been your most memorable business lunch or meeting?

    It would have to be Davos this year, where I joined the UK delegation with Rachel Reeves. The opportunity to be in the room with world leaders and some fascinating people made it an experience I won’t forget.

    And any business faux pas?

    I once found myself at a dinner with a very well-known US political figure who I completely failed to recognise. I asked him his name. He wasn’t impressed.

    What’s been your proudest moment?

    Becoming CEO at 41. Seeing ClearBank grow from a fintech challenger into an established part of the UK’s financial infrastructure has been hugely rewarding. Today, we support more than 300 clients across financial services and the corporate world, have built a profitable UK business and established ourselves in Europe, with plenty more still to do.

    And who do you look up to?

    My dad. He worked incredibly hard and always encouraged me to make the most of every opportunity. Thanks to him, my brother and I were the first in our family to go to university. He taught me the value of hard work, but also the importance of being fair and treating people well.

    What’s the best career advice you’ve ever been given?

    If there’s a fire, run towards it rather than away from it. In other words, don’t shy away from difficult problems. And trust your instincts: keep doing what you think is right until someone tells you to stop.

    And the worst?

    Bang your fists on the table more to get your own way. I’ve always found there are better ways to bring people with you.

    Are you optimistic for the year ahead?

    Yes, always. I’d much rather be optimistic about what’s ahead and risk the odd disappointment than not take the chance at all.

    We’re going for lunch, and you’re picking – where are we going?

    I love a good steak, so I’d go for Gaucho in Broadgate Circus. It also happens to be right next to our new office, which is very convenient.

    And if we’re grabbing a drink after work?

    Any pub on Watling Street. There’s always a great atmosphere after work, you can’t really go wrong.

    Where’s home during the week?

    You’ll mostly find me at ClearBank’s offices in Broadgate Tower. We’re on the 27th floor, with some pretty impressive views across London.

    And where might we find you at the weekend?

    Usually out walking my dog, Maverick, or ferrying my children around. My weekends involve quite a lot of unpaid taxi driving.

    You’ve got a well-deserved two weeks off. Where are you going and who with?

    With two young children, adventure holidays are off the agenda for now. Give me a five-star, all-inclusive resort, a beach and my family, and I’m very happy.
